articles.title: Does Trump’s 60-day tariff waiver really give relief to India? What it means for US trade deal & oil prices - The Times of India
articles.summary: Does Trump’s 60-day tariff waiver really give relief to India? What it means for US trade deal & oil prices  The Times of IndiaOil Futures Pull Back as U.S. Waives Some Russia Sanctions  WSJTrump’s Russian oil waiver may boost India’s winter supplies, but crude prices unlikely to fall  ThePrintRubio says Trump to take up to 60 days to weigh Russia sanctions  ReutersOpinion | Great 'Exceptions': How The Oil India Was Attacked For Is The Oil Trump Now Seeks&...
articles.full_text:
What does US President Donald Trump’s decision to waive sanctions on Russia and tariffs on countries buying oil from Moscow really mean for India? The US decision to waive the proposed sanctions under the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 is clearly aimed at securing relief for its own country.
The development comes amid America’s shifting approach to Russian energy. In a separate deal, Russia agreed to release more than 300,000 metric tonnes of diesel for the US and global markets, with further supplies proposed for subsequent months.
While the US-Russia diesel deal primarily focused on the bilateral US-Russia relations, the tariff waiver is mostly directed to India and China. The threatened 100% tariffs on the five largest buyers of Russian oil and gas were due to take effect 30 days after the legislation’s approval on September 18.
Also Read | 
The return of Middle East oil: Has Iran lost control of Strait of Hormuz & why are crude prices still up?
What Trump has done
Trump invoked Section 115 of the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 to issue the waiver. He certified that it was in the national interest of the US.
"I have submitted to the Congress a certification that the issuance of such a waiver is in the national interests of the United States and a report explaining the basis for the certification, consistent with section 115(b) of the Graham Act," Trump said.
The waiver applies to duties under Sections 112 and 113, which authorised tariffs of up to 500% on goods that are imported from Russia and up to 100% on goods from the five largest buyers of Russian-origin crude oil or natural gas. India and China were among the countries potentially covered by the latter provision.
Trump's sanctions and tariff waiver explained
But, Natalia Katona, Commodity Analyst sees the move as less of a gift to Moscow than an attempt to keep a lid on oil prices.
“Russian crude continued to find buyers despite the tariff threat, effectively the entire November loading programme of Russian export grades has been sold off even though it could’ve been subjected to tariffs,” she tells TOI.
“Enforcing the Lindsey Graham Act would risk disrupting future Russian crude flows and pushing Brent above its current level of around $110 a barrel. With US elections approaching in early November, my reading is that Trump wants to avoid another oil-price shock at all costs,” she says.
What it means for India
For India, the immediate relief is for its crude supply basket and exporters. If India decided to give up Russian crude oil, its single largest supplier would have gone off the table, with no easy replacement amid Middle East tensions. If it continued to buy Russian crude, then the 100% tariffs would have weighed on its exports to the US.
Russian oil supplies to India hit a record high earlier this year when the closure of Strait of Hormuz limited the Middle East crude supplies.
But recently, buying patterns have made a notable shift to the Middle East as supplies through the Strait of Hormuz ease and China begins competing for the same Russian barrels, driving up the cost of oil from Moscow.
Pankaj Srivastava, Senior Vice President, Commodity Market - Oil at Rystad Energy is of the view that India was strategically prepared for the Graham bill, with crude supply from the Middle East rising significantly to approximately 2.5 million bpd in September, while Russian imports declined to around 1.5 million bpd.
The increase in Middle Eastern supply was supported by the continued operation of multiple logistics channels, including the Strait of Hormuz, dark fleet movements, ship-to-ship transfers, alternative Red Sea and Suez Canal routes, and the East-West Pipeline.
“As a result, Middle Eastern crude exports increased to nearly 15 million barrels per day in September, strengthening India's import availability. At the same time, higher insurance and freight costs associated with Black Sea exports, following recent attacks in the region, reduced the competitiveness of Russian crude,” Pankaj Srivastava tells TOI.
According to the expert, with ongoing refinery expansions and strong diesel crack margins supporting exports, the waiver further improves feedstock security for Indian refiners.
“This development is also constructive for global distillate markets and could provide additional support to diesel and jet fuel balances in the US and Europe,” he says.
In addition, Abu Dhabi National Oil Company's decision to align Murban crude pricing with Dubai Platts from 1 November is expected to enhance pricing transparency and improve procurement flexibility for Asian refiners.
“Overall, the combination of the Russian waiver, increased Middle Eastern supply, the UAE's evolving position within OPEC, and the Murban pricing changes is positive for Indian refiners, strengthening their potential to increase diesel and jet fuel exports and generate economic benefits,” he adds.
The caveat
One very important point that is worth noting is that this waiver is for a 60-day period. This is clearly indicative that any relief from sanctions for Russia, and tariffs for countries like India is at best temporary as of now.
A day after suspending sanctions and tariffs linked to Russian exports, US President Donald Trump said on Saturday that he had not yet made a final decision on the issue. Friday's executive order did not specify the duration of the waiver.
What Marco Rubio said about the waiver
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, meanwhile, said the administration wanted additional time to assess the implications of the move.
Rubio said Trump would take up to 60 days to examine the economic consequences of the Russia-related sanctions and tariffs he had waived a day earlier.
Rubio said Trump had chosen to review the measures over a 60-day period.
"I think the president wants to take the 60-day period of time to sort of analyze what imposing both sanctions and tariffs will mean to the global economy and even to the US economy," Rubio said.
Separately, Rubio also appeared to recognise the practical considerations behind India's continued purchases of Russian crude.
The issue has been a key subject of discussions between him and External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar since the US passed the Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act in September.
"You also can't unravel the economy of other countries because of one central issue. So that's the complex part of having to balance all of this,” Rubio said according to PTI.
Jaishankar is understood to have explained to Rubio that Indian refineries are largely designed to process medium-sour crude, which India sources from Middle Eastern countries and Russia.
He is also understood to have pointed out the differences in the grades of oil available from other suppliers. Venezuelan crude is heavier, while US oil is lighter and would need to be blended before Indian refineries could process it.
Will crude oil become cheaper for India?
For India, however, relief from tariffs does not necessarily mean cheaper oil. In fact, even globally despite America’s diesel supply deal with Russia and the sanctions waiver, crude oil prices continue to stay near $110 per barrel.
Pankaj Srivastava says the waiver was largely anticipated and is expected to provide modest support to crude prices while easing supply-side geopolitical risks for India.
As Natalia Katona points out: Removing the threat also removes a potential deterrent for competing buyers of Russian crude.
“So far, purchasing patterns show little sign of changing. For instance, China had already secured November-loading ESPO cargoes by early September, ahead of its usual buying schedule. India’s purchases by mid-October point to Russian crude flows of more or less the same 1.8 million b/d unchanged from September,” she tells TOI.
Brent Crude Price Trends
And, the pricing story is more complicated than the headline premium suggests.
According to Katona, the Urals deliveries to India are generally priced against Dated Brent, which reflects the tight physical crude market.
“Dated Brent was trading $20/bbl above ICE Brent futures for most of October and still is $10/bbl higher, therefore a cargo priced at Dated parity can still carry a substantial premium when compared to any other futures benchmark,” she explains.
Urals has moved from a premium of around $8/bbl to Dated Brent a month ago to roughly Dated parity today, with a possibility for that differential to soften further.
“Russian suppliers are adjusting to a higher physical benchmark and elevated freight costs to keep their barrels competitive. But a falling premium is not the same as a falling oil price,” she notes.
“India may negotiate a better differential with Russian grades and will still face a higher outright bill if the benchmark itself (in this case, Dated Brent) rises. With China competing for Russian barrels and global physical supplies tightening, the waiver eases India’s tariff risk without resolving its supply problem,” she adds.
But the weather may work in India’s favour over the coming months.
In September-October, a total of 12 cargoes carrying Russian oil transited the Northern Sea Route, on their way to China.
According to Katona, these flows should gradually halt as ice takes over most of the Arctic Ocean again, lowering the availability of Urals cargoes for China through the NSR.
“Considering India is generally closer to Russia geographically (entailing a lower freight cost), from November onwards Russian sellers of grades loading in European ports (Urals, Siberian Light or Russian CPC) should have a general prevalence for Indian deliveries,” she believes.

articles.title: India-New Zealand FTA comes into effect, aims to boost exports and investment - ET Manufacturing
articles.summary: India-New Zealand FTA comes into effect, aims to boost exports and investment  ET Manufacturing
articles.full_text:
The India-New Zealand Free Trade Agreement came into effect recently, providing duty-free access to Indian goods. This agreement marks India's 17th Free Trade Agreement, which reinforces its strategic position in the Indo-Pacific.
The India-New Zealand Free Trade Agreement (FTA), signed on April 27, came into effect on Tuesday, providing duty-free access to a range of Indian goods, including products from labour-intensive sectors such as textiles and leather.
It is the seventh trade pact to come into force in the last five years. The others are agreements with the UAE, Mauritius, the European Free Trade Association (EFTA) bloc, the UK, Oman and Australia.
Signed on April 27, 2026, the agreement follows negotiations launched in 2010, stalled in 2015 and revived in March 2025. The pact becomes India's 17th operational FTA.
According to experts, the sectors benefiting from the FTA are textiles and apparel, leather and footwear, engineering goods and auto components, gems and jewellery, agriculture and processed foods, pharmaceuticals, and other manufacturing industries.
New Zealand has committed FDI worth USD 20 billion in over 15 years.
"The FTA's provisions on duty-free access for certain inputs, bilateral cumulation, customs facilitation, and investment-promotion mechanisms may encourage deeper value-chain integration and improve investment conditions," he said.
He added that the pact has significance beyond trade, strengthening India's strategic position in the Indo-Pacific, expanding its network of FTAs with developed economies.
At a time of growing global trade uncertainty, the India-New Zealand FTA is a strong endorsement of open markets and predictable trade rules. Its target of doubling bilateral trade by 2030 sets an ambitious agenda for both countries.
What makes this FTA particularly valuable is that it goes beyond goods to cover services, investment, skills and mobility, creating fresh opportunities for Indian professionals and businesses.
With 100 per cent of Indian exports gaining duty-free access to New Zealand from day one, the agreement gives Indian exporters a significant competitive advantage. MSMEs in textiles, leather, footwear and engineering goods are particularly well placed to benefit.
Economic think tank Chintan Research Foundation (CRF India) President Shishir Priyadarshi said that at a time of growing global trade uncertainty, the India-New Zealand FTA is a strong endorsement of open markets and predictable trade rules.
"What makes this FTA particularly valuable is that it goes beyond goods to cover services, investment, skills and mobility, creating fresh opportunities for Indian professionals and businesses," he said.
Trade expert and Hi-Tech Gears Chairman Deep Kapuria said the FTA operationalisation with New Zealand completes India's preferential market access in all major countries of the Asia-Pacific region.
"New Zealand is a very open economy; India has very well crafted this trade deal by securing market access for new services such as Ayush, yoga instructors and student mobility, including post-study work visa," he said.
Bilateral trade declined by about 11 per cent to USD 1.15 billion in 2025-26 from USD 1.3 billion in the previous fiscal year. India's exports stood at USD 566.51 million, while imports were USD 589.1 million, resulting in a meagre trade deficit of USD 22.59 million for India.
Rani Singh, Indian-origin New Zealander, said the deal is an important step forward for both countries as it is not just about trade; it is about bringing the two countries closer, creating opportunities for businesses and people, and building a stronger relationship for the future.
"India now has an opportunity to build its own strong partnership with New Zealand. With duty-free access to New Zealand for all Indian export tariff lines from day one, Indian businesses can become more competitive in this market," she said.
Singh added that the benefits are not limited to goods as there is also scope for greater cooperation in education, tourism, technology, professional services and investment.
Greater opportunities for eligible skilled professionals and young people can further strengthen these connections, she said.

articles.title: New Zealand’s trade pact with India removes tariffs on 57% of its exports - Vinetur
articles.summary: New Zealand’s trade pact with India removes tariffs on 57% of its exports  Vinetur
articles.full_text:
The deal lifts India’s 33% sheepmeat duty immediately, with duty-free access rising to 82% by 2027
Tuesday, October 20, 2026
New Zealand’s free trade agreement with India took effect on Tuesday, immediately removing Indian tariffs on 57% of New Zealand exports to that market and beginning a phased reduction of steep duties on products such as wine, honey and infant formula.
New Zealand’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade said the agreement entered into force on October 20, one month after Trade and Investment Minister Todd McClay and India’s High Commissioner to New Zealand, Muanpuii Saiawi, exchanged ratification documents at Parliament. The deal was signed in New Delhi on April 27 by McClay and Indian Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal after negotiations that began in March 2025 and concluded in December of that year.
The agreement marks one of New Zealand’s fastest trade negotiations with India. McClay told Radio New Zealand that the share of New Zealand exports entering India duty-free will rise to 82% as the pact is phased in, with the next round of tariff cuts scheduled for January 1, 2027. He said the two countries finished the talks in nine months, which he described as a record for India on a comprehensive trade agreement.
The products receiving immediate tariff-free treatment include sheepmeat, wool and coal. The Ministry’s outcomes summary says India’s 33% tariff on sheepmeat was removed on day one, while more than 95% of New Zealand forestry and wood exports now enter India duty-free. Tariffs of 33% on key fish and seafood lines will be phased out over seven years, and most industrial products will become tariff-free within 10 years. Once the agreement is fully implemented, the ministry says the average tariff applied to New Zealand’s current exports to India will fall to 3%.
Agricultural access is uneven across sectors. Horticulture gains quota-based access rather than full liberalization. New Zealand became the first country to secure preferential access for apples in an Indian trade agreement. India’s 50% tariff on apples will be cut in half within a quota that McClay said in July starts at 32,500 tonnes and rises to 45,000 tonnes by year six. Kiwifruit will receive a duty-free quota starting at 6,250 tonnes and rising to 15,000 tonnes, while the 33% tariff will be cut in half for shipments above that level.
Those quotas were set above recent trade volumes. McClay said in July that apple shipments to India were up 63% from the 2024 season and that India had risen from New Zealand’s seventh-largest apple market to its fourth-largest in two years.
Wine faces a slower path. India’s 150% tariff on New Zealand wine will be reduced over 10 years, with the final rate falling to either 25% or 50% depending on the price band. The first cut took effect Tuesday. The agreement also includes a most-favored-nation provision for wine, meaning any better deal India gives another wine-producing country will automatically apply to New Zealand. That matters because the European Union has already negotiated a lower rate with India.
For the beverage industry, the tariff phase-down opens a market that has been largely closed to New Zealand wine because of price barriers. The change could lead New Zealand wineries, distributors and importers to reassess pricing and brand positioning in India against Australian and European competitors as duties fall over time, although the pace of change will depend on how quickly tariffs come down and how producers build distribution.
New Zealand Winegrowers Chief Executive Philip Gregan said in April that India represented “a significant long-term opportunity” for the country’s wine sector. The industry body said wine exports to India were slightly below NZ$300,000 in 2025, reflecting the effect of the tariff wall.
Honey exporters also gained a limited opening. The 66% tariff on manuka honey will fall by three quarters to 16.5% over five years for honey certified by New Zealand’s Ministry for Primary Industries and priced at or above US$30 a kilogram. The ministry said this is the first time India has granted preferential access for honey to any country. Recent exports averaged only 7 tonnes a year.
Dairy, which became a central political issue during the debate over the agreement, remains mostly outside the deal. New Zealand did not secure new access for milk, cheese or butter. It did obtain a seven-year phaseout of India’s 33% tariff on bulk infant formula and other dairy-based food preparations, plus a new 3,000-tonne quota for albumins with the tariff halved to 11%. The agreement also includes a fast-track arrangement that allows Indian manufacturers to import New Zealand ingredients duty-free for products they later export.
India also agreed to consult New Zealand if it offers dairy access in the future to another comparable country, and both governments will review the entire agreement one year after it entered into force.
Meat industry groups welcomed the agreement when it was signed, while warning that gains would not be immediate. Meat Industry Association Chair Nathan Guy said in April that India was a market with “significant long-term potential” but that the agreement would not bring quick results. Beef + Lamb New Zealand Chair Kate Acland said rising incomes in India were likely to increase demand for higher-quality protein.
On New Zealand’s side, the agreement eliminates tariffs on 100% of Indian goods from Tuesday. Those tariffs had been as high as 10%. The ministry said consumers and businesses in New Zealand should see lower prices on some imports from India, including textiles, fabric, machinery and electrical goods.
The deal also includes mobility and investment provisions that have drawn political scrutiny. It provides up to 1,667 temporary three-year employment entry visas a year for Indian workers, with a cap of 5,000 holders at any one time. Of those annual places, 1,467 are tied to 13 skill-shortage occupations on New Zealand’s Green List, while 200 are reserved for chefs, yoga instructors, music teachers and Ayurveda practitioners. A separate working holiday scheme will allow up to 1,000 Indians ages 18 to 30 to travel and work in New Zealand each year.
New Zealand has also committed to promote US$20 billion in private investment into India over 15 years, while India will create a New Zealand Investment Desk to support those investors. The agreement does not include investor-state dispute settlement.
Those migration and investment terms helped shape the domestic political debate in New Zealand. Parliament passed the implementing legislation in September by 93 votes to 29. New Zealand First voted against it. Foreign Minister Winston Peters, whose party opposed the legislation, called the agreement “a bad deal for New Zealand” when negotiations concluded last December, arguing that it gave too much away on immigration while delivering too little on dairy. Labour supported the legislation but raised concerns about the migration and investment chapters.
The review built into the agreement will take place after New Zealand’s election on November 7, leaving the next government to assess how the pact is working in practice.
Trade between the two countries remains modest by New Zealand’s standards. The ministry said two-way trade totaled NZ$3.68 billion in the year to June 2025. New Zealand exported NZ$1.79 billion in goods and services to India and imported NZ$1.88 billion. India was New Zealand’s 12th-largest export market and accounted for just over 1.5% of its total exports.
The largest single New Zealand export to India was not a farm product but travel services, worth NZ$948 million, which reflects spending by Indian students and visitors in New Zealand. Forestry contributed NZ$134 million, horticulture NZ$118 million, iron and steel NZ$84 million, and wool NZ$76 million.
McClay has framed the agreement as part of the government’s goal of doubling the value of New Zealand’s exports within 10 years. He told RNZ that the pact’s entry into force was “a big step” toward that target and argued that early access matters as India’s economy expands.

articles.title: India–New Zealand FTA to Take Effect on 20 October 2026 on Vijay Dashmi, Unlocking 100% Duty-Free Market Access, New Export Opportunities and USD 20 Billion Investment Potential - A2Z Taxcorp LLP
articles.summary: India–New Zealand FTA to Take Effect on 20 October 2026 on Vijay Dashmi, Unlocking 100% Duty-Free Market Access, New Export Opportunities and USD 20 Billion Investment Potential  A2Z Taxcorp LLP
articles.full_text:
Union Minister of Commerce and Industry Shri Piyush Goyal and New Zealand’s Minister for Trade and Investment, Hon. Todd McClay, today jointly announced through a virtual conference that the India–New Zealand Free Trade Agreement (FTA) will enter into force on 20 October 2026, on the occasion of Vijay Dashmi, a day symbolising victory and new beginnings..
Speaking on the occasion, Union Minister of Commerce and Industry Shri Piyush Goyal said, “Ours is a winning partnership, both on and off the field. The success of this agreement will be measured by the opportunities it creates and the difference it makes to the lives of the people of New Zealand and India. For India, 100% duty-free access to the New Zealand market opens significant new opportunities for our exporters, particularly MSMEs, artisans, farmers, and women entrepreneurs. For our farmers, the agreement combines new opportunities with appropriate safeguards. The Agricultural Productivity Partnership, with action plans for apples, kiwifruit and honey, establishment of Centres of Excellence, promote better orchard management, reduce post-harvest losses, and improve agricultural productivity, supporting stronger farm incomes across the country. The agreement also aligns with the vision of our Hon’ble Prime Minister for Viksit Bharat 2047: that is a developed and prosperous India built on competitiveness, innovation, productive capacity, and inclusive prosperity when India celebrates 100 years of independence.”
New Zealand’s Minister for Trade and Investment, Hon. Todd McClay, stated, “The entry into force of India-New Zealand Free Trade Agreement is a watershed moment in the relationship between our two countries. For New Zealand exporters, the FTA opens the door to 1.4 billion consumers and one of the world’s fastest-growing major economies. New Zealand’s current exports to India will benefit from tariff elimination or substantial tariff reductions. At the same time, all Indian goods will be able to enter New Zealand duty-free, creating new opportunities for Indian exporters and placing them on a level playing field with New Zealand’s other FTA partners. The success of this agreement will ultimately be measured by the opportunities it creates and the extent to which our businesses use it.”
Secretary, Department of Commerce, Shri Rajesh Agrawal, said, “FTAs are about creating a deep economic partnership between countries. As a part of the FTA, we see this partnership also driving a lot of New Zealand investment in India. All the other big economies around the Pacific have got a much deeper trade with New Zealand. This FTA opens up the opportunity that we can also be a major contributor to the bilateral trade between India and New Zealand. The job is now to translate this opportunity into actual benefits for our people. We are working with all the Industry and the associations to take this message forward to every district across the country.”
Under the leadership of Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi, India and New Zealand have continued to deepen and expand their engagement. The FTA reflects India’s commitment to forging partnerships with developed economies that deliver market access, create employment opportunities and empower youth, women and MSMEs, in line with the vision of Viksit Bharat 2047
Representatives from industries in India and New Zealand also participated in the ceremony and spoke about opportunities created by the Agreement for their respective sectors, including services, footwear, engineering and agriculture.
On the occasion, the first-ever export of a JCB machine from India to New Zealand was flagged off by the Union Minister of Commerce and Industry. Flag-offs of a range of products across the agriculture, gems and jewellery, engineering, sporting goods, footwear and leather sectors are also planned for the entry-into-force day. These initiatives reflect the confidence of Indian manufacturers and the opportunities the Agreement opens up for exporters across the country.
New Zealand has eliminated customs duties on all tariff lines covering Indian exports, removing peak tariffs of up to 10%. Textiles, apparel, leather, footwear, gems and jewellery, engineering goods, automobiles and auto components, chemicals, pharmaceuticals, agricultural products and processed foods are expected to benefit. Duty-free access for wooden logs, coking coal and metal waste and scrap will further strengthen manufacturing and MSME supply chains. The pharmaceutical and medical device industries will benefit from streamlined regulatory processes.
New Zealand has made its best services offer in any of its trade agreements to date, with market access in around 118 sectors and Most-Favoured-Nation commitments in about 139 sub-sectors. For the first time, it has also provided dedicated access in Health and Traditional Medicine Services, covering Ayurveda, Yoga and other AYUSH systems.
Indian youth and professionals will have access to a quota of 5,000 Temporary Employment Entry visas and 1,000 Working Holiday visas every year. There will be no numerical cap on Indian students, with post-study work rights of up to three years for STEM Bachelor’s and Master’s graduates and up to four years for doctoral scholars.
The Agricultural Productivity Partnership is a key component of the Agreement, extending cooperation beyond tariff concessions to bring global technology, training and best practices to Indian farmers. It includes dedicated Action Plans for kiwifruit, apples and honey, with cooperation also extending to horticulture, forestry, livestock and fisheries.
New Zealand is providing technical assistance for establishing Centres of Excellence for kiwifruit, apples and honey. Under the Kiwifruit Action Plan, Phase I sites have been identified at Pfutsero in Nagaland and Magra in Uttarakhand. Two further Centres of Excellence for apples are proposed in Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand, while the Honey Action Plan envisages Centres of Excellence in Uttar Pradesh and West Bengal. These initiatives aim to support farmers through technology transfer, improved cultivation practices and enhanced productivity.
Representatives from Himachal Pradesh, Nagaland, Uttarakhand, Uttar Pradesh and Arunachal Pradesh, along with collaborating organisations from New Zealand, were present for the entry into force.
All Tariff Rate Quotas for apples, kiwifruit and Mānuka honey are formally linked to the delivery of the Action Plans, under the oversight of a Joint Agriculture Productivity Council. This links market access with farmer welfare.
New Zealand has committed to facilitate USD 20 billion of investment into India. The investment is expected to benefit agriculture, manufacturing, infrastructure and start-ups, and support innovation, entrepreneurship and employment generation under the Make in India vision.
To protect farmers, dairy producers, fisherfolk and rural communities, sensitive products such as dairy, sugar, edible oils and key agricultural commodities remain excluded from concessions. Robust Rules of Origin, a bilateral safeguard mechanism and strong anti-circumvention provisions will ensure that the benefits flow only to genuine Indian exporters.
The Agreement opens an advanced overseas market to India’s MSMEs, women-led enterprises, start-ups, artisans and first-generation entrepreneurs. Zero duty and faster customs processes will lower landed costs and widen their customer base. Structured cooperation will provide enhanced access to trade-related information and linkages with New Zealand’s SME ecosystem, with a specific focus on enterprises owned by women and youth.
New Zealand has also committed to facilitate the registration of Indian Geographical Indications, opening avenues for protection of products associated with rural artisans and traditional industries.
The India–New Zealand FTA is a people-centric and inclusive partnership, anchored in the vision of Viksit Bharat 2047 and the leadership of Hon’ble Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi. It seeks to empower farmers, MSMEs, women-led enterprises, entrepreneurs, artisans, youth and professionals.
Negotiations were launched on 16 March 2025 and concluded on 22 December 2025, within nine months. The Agreement was signed on 27 April 2026. It supports the India–New Zealand Strategic Partnership: Roadmap to 2030, which sets an aspirational goal of doubling bilateral trade in goods and services to NZ$7 billion (₹35,000 crore) by 2030.

articles.title: India Connects Kashmir, Builds the Infrastructure for Growth - Jharkhand State News
articles.summary: India Connects Kashmir, Builds the Infrastructure for Growth  Jharkhand State News
articles.full_text:
Jammu and Kashmir's challenging terrain is steadily yielding to a new era of connectivity. The Udhampur–Srinagar–Baramulla Rail Link has connected the valley to India's rail network. Its centrepiece, the Chenab Bridge, stands as the world's highest railway arch bridge. Expanded Vande Bharat services are improving passenger mobility. New freight terminals are carrying Kashmiri apples, saffron and handicrafts to national markets, opening opportunities for farmers and businesses. On land, the Sonamarg and Zojila tunnels promise year-round passage into Ladakh. In the air, Srinagar's expanding airport is complemented by nascent hubs at Udhampur and Kishtwar. Together, these advances are drawing Kashmir's produce, trade and tourism firmly into the national mainstream.
A Region Reconnected
Jammu and Kashmir's mountainous terrain has long made connectivity a major infrastructure challenge. Over the years, this has been steadily changing, with a wave of infrastructure investment reshaping how the region connects with the rest of the country. The Udhampur–Srinagar–Baramulla Rail Link (USBRL) project is a major part of this expansion. It is one of the most challenging railway line projects undertaken in the country post-independence. Today it stands as one of India’s engineering marvels, linking the Kashmir Valley to the rest of the country by rail.
The USBRL project has also been accompanied by sustained expansion of roads, tunnels and airport infrastructure. The network now includes new train services such as the Vande Bharat Express. It also includes major road corridors and tunnels. Airport capacity is being expanded at Srinagar, with regional airports planned under UDAN, increasing passenger movement. Multimodal cargo terminals and enhanced freight services support goods movement across the region. These developments have progressively expanded all-weather connectivity infrastructure across Jammu and Kashmir.
Railways: Connecting Kashmir to the National Rail Network
Udhampur-Srinagar-Baramulla Rail Link (USBRL) National Project
The USBRL project was inaugurated in June 2025, improving connectivity infrastructure in the Himalayan region. Built at a cost of ₹43,780 crore, the USBRL project covers the districts of Udhampur, Reasi, Ramban, Srinagar, Anantnag, Pulwama, Budgam and Baramulla of Jammu and Kashmir.
The project stretches 272 kilometres through the rugged Himalayas; it includes 36 tunnels that span 119 kilometres and 943 bridges. Designed to overcome the region’s challenging terrain, it connects remote areas with the national rail network. It is opening new opportunities for mobility, trade and tourism. As part of the USBRL project, over 215 km (including a tunnel and 320 bridges) of roads have been constructed, which are useful for communities. Additionally, the USBRL project is fully electrified both in tunnels and in open stretches.
The USBRL project has made substantial socio-economic contributions to the region, with employment generation being a significant aspect of its impact. The project has generated more than 5 crore man-days of employment.
Vande Bharat Express
Vande Bharat Express, Jammu and Kashmir
The Vande Bharat Express in Jammu and Kashmir first began operations in June 2025, between Katra and Srinagar. To further enhance railway connectivity, the Srinagar-Katra Vande Bharat Express service was extended to Jammu Tawi Railway Station in April 2026.
The distance from Jammu to Srinagar is now covered in less than five hours. The trains have been augmented from 8 to 20 coaches. They are specially designed to operate in extreme weather conditions. The trains are equipped with advanced operating systems and electronics suited for high-altitude conditions.
Supporting this route is a snow removal train that moves ahead to clear the tracks, ensuring year-round services. Seismic dampers have also been installed to absorb tremors, offering a safer and smoother journey in this high-risk zone.
Engineering Marvels under the USBRL Project
The USBRL project includes several major engineering achievements, including the Chenab Rail Bridge, Anji Khad Bridge and Tunnel T50.
Chenab Rail Bridge
Under the USBRL project, the world’s highest railway arch bridge has been built over the Chenab River in the Reasi district of Jammu and Kashmir. The Chenab bridge, inaugurated in June 2025, is 1,315 m long. It has an arch span of 467 metres and rises 359 metres above the riverbed, making it higher than the Eiffel Tower. The bridge is designed to withstand strong seismic and wind forces. With Vande Bharat services running over the bridge, connectivity has significantly improved between Jammu and Kashmir.

Anji Khad Bridge in Jammu and Kashmir
The Anji Khad bridge is India’s first cable-stayed railway bridge built above the Anji River gorge, a tributary of the Chenab River. The Anji Khad bridge is part of the USBRL project and was inaugurated in June 2025.
The bridge is located in the Reasi district of Jammu and Kashmir. It is supported by a single 193-metre-high tower shaped like an inverted ‘Y’, with cables supporting the bridge. The main bridge has a total length of 473.25 metres, designed for the region’s challenging terrain and seismic conditions.
Tunnel T50 in Jammu and Kashmir
Tunnel T50, inaugurated in 2024, is a 12.77-km rail tunnel linking Khari and Sumber in Jammu and Kashmir. It is India’s longest transportation tunnel, built under the USBRL project. The tunnel provides a vital rail link between the Kashmir Valley and the rest of India.
The New Austrian Tunnelling Method has been used to construct the tunnel through the challenging Himalayan geology. The tunnel engineering overcame the challenges of high-water ingress, landslides, shear zones, and jointed volcanic rocks. The tunnel features a main tube paired with a parallel escape tunnel, linked every 375 metres for safety. CCTV cameras are placed every 50 metres, which help monitor from a central control room.

Railway connectivity in Jammu and Kashmir is being strengthened through increased investment in supporting infrastructure and network development. The annual average budget of railways for Jammu and Kashmir has increased from ₹1,044 crore in 2009–14 to ₹1,086 crore in 2026–27.
Electrification
Indian Railways has pursued railway electrification in mission mode, with about 99.6% of the Broad Gauge (BG) network now electrified. In Jammu and Kashmir, the entire existing BG network is electrified. All new-line and multi-tracking projects are being sanctioned and built with electrification from the outset.
Station Redevelopment
Under the Amrit Bharat Station Scheme, 1,340 stations have been identified for redevelopment across Indian Railways. Among them, four stations are in Jammu and Kashmir. The stations are Budgam, Jammu Tawi, Martyr Captain Tushar Mahajan (Udhampur) and Shri Mata Vaishno Devi Katra station.
Other Regional Railway Initiatives

Roads as a complement to Rail
In Jammu and Kashmir, road infrastructure is expanding alongside railway infrastructure. Roads remain essential for last-mile access to places outside the railway network. In August 2026, foundation stones were laid for 110 road projects covering 598.455 km under Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana (PMGSY)-IV. Costing more than ₹1,500 crore, the projects are expected to benefit 46,972 people across the Udhampur–Kathua–Doda–Kishtwar region. The projects also include the use of waste plastics in several road packages, supporting more sustainable road construction.
Tunnel construction has also become a key component of development in the Himalayan region to ensure all-weather connectivity, improve road safety, and enhance strategic mobility.
Sonamarg Tunnel, Jammu and Kashmir
The Sonamarg tunnel project, also known as the Z-Morh, inaugurated in January 2025, is a 6.4 km bi-directional tunnel with a parallel escape tunnel of length 6.4 km and an approach road of length 5.5km. Constructed at a cost of over ₹2,700 crore, the tunnel sits at an altitude of 2634 meters above sea level. The tunnel provides all-weather connectivity between Srinagar and Sonamarg enroute to Leh. It bypasses parts of the road hit by major avalanches and landslides. It promotes tourism by transforming Sonamarg into a year-round destination, boosting winter tourism, adventure sports and local livelihoods. Along with the Zojila Tunnel, it will cut the NH-1 section of this project from 13 km to 11.98 km.
Zojila Tunnel

articles.title: ‘Deal pretty close’: Trump on India-US trade agreement - The Siasat Daily
articles.summary: ‘Deal pretty close’: Trump on India-US trade agreement  The Siasat Daily
articles.full_text:
Washington: US President Donald Trump said that India wants to conclude a trade agreement with the United States and indicated that the two countries were close to reaching a deal, while suggesting that the final arrangement would differ significantly from earlier trade agreements.
Speaking to reporters during an Oval Office interaction alongside Vice President JD Vance, Trump responded to a question about whether Washington and New Delhi were approaching an agreement.
“They want to make a deal. We’re going to make a deal pretty close,” Trump said.
“Yeah, that’s going to be a much different kind of deal than we’ve made,” he added.
The remarks came as Secretary of State Marco Rubio was visiting India and holding discussions with External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar, placing the President’s comments against the backdrop of high-level diplomatic engagement between the two countries.
Trump did not elaborate on what would make the proposed agreement different from previous arrangements.
He also did not specify a date for concluding negotiations or identify the remaining issues preventing a final agreement.
The President’s comments nevertheless suggested that Washington expected progress in talks that have been closely watched by businesses, exporters and investors in both countries.
India and the United States have been negotiating a bilateral trade arrangement aimed at expanding market access and addressing longstanding differences over tariffs, agricultural products, industrial goods and regulatory barriers.
Trade negotiations have acquired additional significance under Trump’s second administration, which has made tariffs and reciprocal market access central elements of American economic policy.
The administration has argued that trading partners must offer American businesses greater access to their markets while reducing barriers affecting US exports.
For India, the negotiations carry implications for major export sectors, including pharmaceuticals, engineering goods, textiles, electronics and information technology-related services.
American companies have also sought greater opportunities in India’s expanding consumer market and manufacturing sectors.
The President’s latest remarks did not indicate whether negotiators had resolved differences over specific sectors or reached agreement on tariff reductions.
Nor did he announce any new investment commitments, market-access concessions or implementation timetable.
The comments came during an Oval Office event primarily devoted to the administration’s efforts to combat fraud involving federal government programmes.
Trump and Vance announced new incentives for individuals reporting suspected misuse of taxpayer funds and discussed the administration’s broader economic priorities.
During the interaction, Trump also spoke about reducing American trade deficits with major trading partners.
He cited Canada, Mexico and the European Union while arguing that his administration’s trade policies were changing longstanding commercial relationships.
The President said the United States was experiencing strong economic growth and attracting substantial new investment in manufacturing and industrial facilities.
He presented the administration’s tariff and trade strategy as part of a wider effort to strengthen domestic production and employment.
Although Trump did not discuss India’s tariffs or trade surplus during the exchange, his remarks about the proposed agreement came within that broader economic context.
The President’s comments followed months of discussions between officials in Washington and New Delhi over the terms of a bilateral trade arrangement.
Both governments have identified trade and investment as important pillars of the relationship, alongside defence cooperation, technology partnerships and energy security.
The United States is among India’s largest trading partners, with bilateral commerce spanning goods and services. The economic relationship also includes substantial investment flows and commercial partnerships involving technology, pharmaceuticals, manufacturing and financial services.

articles.title: ‘Tariffs Are Not Meant To Punish India’: Marco Rubio Says US-India Trade Deal Is Close - Outlook India
articles.summary: ‘Tariffs Are Not Meant To Punish India’: Marco Rubio Says US-India Trade Deal Is Close  Outlook India
articles.full_text:
- Marco Rubio says US tariffs on India are part of Washington’s broader foreign policy response to Russia’s war against Ukraine, not an attempt to punish New Delhi.
- The US secretary of state says the India-US trade agreement is close to completion, although some issues remain unresolved.
- Russian oil imports, immigration restrictions and visa policies remain points of friction as the two countries seek to strengthen their strategic and economic partnership.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has said American tariffs on India were not intended to “punish or harm” the country, arguing that the measures form part of Washington’s wider foreign policy response to Russia’s war against Ukraine. Speaking during his visit to India, Rubio said the United States wanted the conflict to end, as New Delhi and Washington work to finalise a long-delayed trade agreement amid tensions over tariffs and India’s purchases of Russian oil.
“None of these tariffs are done to punish or harm India,” Rubio said in an interview with The Indian Express, adding that they were part of a broader foreign policy approach shaped by the war in Ukraine. His remarks appeared aimed at addressing Indian concerns over US trade measures, which have complicated efforts to strengthen economic ties between the two countries.
Trade Deal Nears Completion Amid Tariff Dispute
Rubio said the India-US trade agreement was “incredibly close” to completion, with most of the work finished and only a small number of issues remaining. The negotiations have been underway for more than a year and a half, but progress has been held up by disagreements over tariffs, market access and India’s continued purchases of Russian crude. Rubio’s comments suggest both sides are seeking to move past the dispute, although no final agreement has been announced.
During his Mumbai visit, Rubio held talks with External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar on trade, energy, defence, technology and regional developments. The two sides also discussed strengthening the wider strategic partnership. The talks came days after US President Donald Trump waived potential additional tariffs linked to India’s Russian oil purchases, easing one immediate source of pressure on bilateral trade negotiations.
Russian Oil And Visa Restrictions Remain Points Of Friction
India’s purchases of Russian crude have been a major source of tension with Washington since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. The US has pressed countries to reduce their reliance on Russian energy as part of efforts to limit Moscow’s revenue, while India has defended its energy decisions on the grounds of national interest and supply security. Rubio’s comments acknowledge the geopolitical context of the tariffs but do not remove the wider differences between the two countries over energy and trade.
Rubio also defended the Trump administration’s immigration restrictions, saying they were intended to address longstanding weaknesses in the US immigration system rather than target India specifically. His comments come amid Indian concerns over visa policies and their impact on skilled workers and technology companies. The trade negotiations, energy cooperation and immigration rules remain important tests for a relationship both governments describe as strategically significant.
As Rubio continues his India visit, the immediate challenge for both governments is to translate the improved tone into progress on outstanding economic issues. His assurance that the tariffs were not intended as punishment signals an effort to ease tensions, but the durability of the reset will depend on whether the two sides can conclude the trade agreement and manage their differences over Russia, energy and immigration.

articles.title: Marco Rubio In India: Can US Biz Diplomacy Ease Trump Tensions Over Tariffs, Russian Oil And Bring Trade Deal Closer? - Menafn

Rubio, who arrived in Mumbai on October 20 for a three-day visit, described India as a global“refining superpower” and said Washington would discuss opportunities for Reliance to process more Venezuelan crude at its Indian refineries.
He also indicated that the Indian conglomerate could explore producing oil in Venezuela.
The visit comes at a sensitive juncture in India-US relations, with trade disputes and tariff tensions persisting even as New Delhi continues to buy Russian crude to diversify its energy supplies and safeguard its energy security.
However, US President Donald Trump 's recent decision to waive potential sanctions-related tariffs on major buyers of Russian crude could remove one significant obstacle to a bilateral trade agreement, as per Reuters report.
Against this backdrop, Rubio's engagements with External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar in Mumbai and Reliance Industries chairman Mukesh Ambani in Jamnagar underscore the importance Washington is placing on commercial and energy diplomacy alongside its broader strategic partnership with India.
India-US trade deal: 'Very, very close', says Rubio
Rubio struck an optimistic note on the long-pending India-US trade agreement, saying the negotiations were nearing completion, with only a few issues left to resolve.
“We're very, very close. I would say we're about as close as you can be without having executed the agreement,” Rubio told reporters in Mumbai on Tuesday.
Following the meeting between Jaishankar and Rubio, the Ministry of External Affairs (MEA ) said the two sides discussed a broad range of issues, including trade, defence, technology and energy security.
“They welcomed the progress made in negotiations on the India–U.S. Bilateral Trade Agreement (BTA ) and reaffirmed their commitment to working towards its early conclusion,” the MEA said in a statement.
The ministers also exchanged views on regional and global developments, according to the ministry.
Why is Rubio visiting Mumbai and Jamnagar instead of Delhi?
One of the most striking aspects of Rubio's itinerary is its emphasis on India's and industrial centres rather than New Delhi, where high-level diplomatic engagements with visiting US officials would ordinarily be expected to take place.
Mumbai provides access to corporate leaders and financial institutions, while Jamnagar in Gujarat is home to Reliance Industries' twin refineries, which together form the world's largest single-location refining complex.
Also Read | India-US trade deal 'very close' to completion, Marco Rubio says
US Ambassador to India Sergio Gor has said that the visit would have a stronger focus, with Rubio scheduled to meet government officials in Mumbai and business representatives in Jamnagar.
Suresh K Goel, a former Indian diplomat, said the choice of locations raised questions about the nature of the visit and the agenda behind the engagements.
“If the Ministry of External Affairs prepared the programme, I do find it that this meeting was not scheduled earlier in Delhi and that he was going to Mumbai or to Jamnagar. Clearly, the agenda for the meeting was not official talks or anything,” Goel told LiveMint.
Why is Reliance Industries important to the US energy agenda?
Rubio's planned engagement with Reliance highlights the role India's refining capacity could play in Washington's efforts to expand markets for Venezuelan crude.
The US secretary of state said Washington would discuss encouraging Reliance to refine more Venezuelan oil at its Indian facilities and potentially explore oil production opportunities in Venezuela.
Reliance operates a massive refining complex in Jamnagar, giving it the capacity to process a wide range of crude grades. Its role could therefore be significant in any effort to expand the flow of Venezuelan oil to India.
For Washington, the discussions offer a potential commercial avenue for strengthening energy ties with India.
Rubio's visit is also expected to include a meeting with Reliance chairman Mukesh Ambani, bringing one of India's largest corporate groups into discussions that extend beyond conventional government-to-government diplomacy.
Russian oil, Trump's tariff threat and the road to a trade deal
Trump's administration had authorised the possibility of imposing tariffs of up to 100% on major importers of Russian oil, a measure that could have affected India, the world's second-largest buyer of Russian crude after China.
However, Trump recently waived potential tariffs targeting major buyers of Russian oil, removing one possible stumbling block in the trade negotiations with New Delhi, as per a Reuters report.
The move has also drawn criticism from US lawmakers who argue that Washington has been insufficiently tough on Moscow.
Why the strategic partnership still matters
Despite the strains over trade and Russian oil, India remains an important partner for the United States because of its economic potential, democratic institutions and cooperation across multiple strategic sectors, according to Goel.
Goel cautioned against allowing trade disputes or differences in diplomatic approach to overshadow the broader relationship.
“The relationship between India and the USA is very, very important in all respects. And therefore, the government, rather than becoming part of this temperament or trade effect kind of a thing, has to be mature in our dealing and try and see how we can actually conduct the relationship,” Goel told LiveMint.
He also emphasised India's significance as a democratic and economic partner for Washington in Asia.
“India continues to be important for the USA as an economic and democratic partner. After all, if you look at Asia, which is the other democracy which can compare in terms of relationship?” Goel said.

Rubio hails oil diversification progress
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio arrived in Mumbai on Tuesday for a three-day visit, declaring that a comprehensive trade agreement with India was "very close" while praising New Delhi's efforts to reduce dependence on Russian energy supplies. Speaking to reporters in India's financial capital, Rubio noted that diversifying energy sources "is not easy to do... from one day to the next," but added that Indian officials had expressed "repeatedly... their desire to diversify their energy portfolio, which is a smart thing to do." Trade negotiations in final stages

Tariff uncertainties loom

articles.title: India's FTA Sprint: How a Year of Trade Diplomacy Is Reshaping the Growth Story - cfo.economictimes.indiatimes.com
articles.summary: India's FTA Sprint: How a Year of Trade Diplomacy Is Reshaping the Growth Story  cfo.economictimes.indiatimes.com
articles.full_text:
In the last one year, India has signed, concluded, or advanced more trade agreements than in any comparable period in its post-liberalisation history. In roughly twelve months, New Delhi has taken the India–UK Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA) from signature to entry into force, brought the India–EFTA Trade and Economic Partnership Agreement (TEPA) into effect, sealed a Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA) with Oman, concluded a Free Trade Agreement with New Zealand, closed out nearly two decades of on-and-off negotiations with the European Union, delivered a framework for an interim trade arrangement with the United States, and launched formal FTA talks with the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) bloc and the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU).
India's approach to Free Trade Agreements (FTAs) has undergone a significant transformation over the past decade. While the earlier generation of FTAs primarily focused on tariff liberalization and expanding market access, the recent agreements signed since 2025 reflect a broader strategic objective i.e. integrating India into global value chains (GVCs), attracting investments, strengthening domestic manufacturing and positioning India as a trusted global supply chain hub.
The First Generation of FTAs: Trade-Centric Agreements
India's earlier FTAs with ASEAN, Japan, South Korea, Sri Lanka, Singapore and MERCOSUR were negotiated during a period when the country's primary objective was to expand merchandise trade by reducing import duties. These agreements largely concentrated on:
* Tariff reduction on goods
* Limited coverage of services and investment
* Restricted provisions on digital trade, sustainability and government procurement
* Minimal emphasis on supply chain resilience or technology collaboration
Although these agreements improved bilateral trade, several faced criticisms due to rising imports without a proportionate increase in India's exports. Concerns were also raised over widening trade deficits, inadequate Rules of Origin enforcement and limited utilization by Indian exporters, particularly MSMEs.
The Shift in India's Trade Strategy
The global economic landscape has changed considerably since the COVID-19 pandemic. Geopolitical realignments, supply chain disruptions, protectionist measures and the global "China+1" manufacturing strategy have compelled India to rethink its trade policy.
Consequently, India's recent FTAs represent a shift from "market access" to "strategic economic integration." Instead of viewing FTAs merely as instruments for lowering tariffs, they are increasingly being used as catalysts for investment, technology transfer, industrial development and export competitiveness.
Why now? Reading the strategy behind the surge
Three forces appear to be driving this compressed burst of dealmaking:
1. De-risking from a single-market dependency. With US tariff actions creating unpredictability for Indian exporters - particularly in textiles, gems and engineering goods, diversifying market access across the UK, EU, EFTA, Oceania and the Gulf reduces India's exposure to any one trading partner's policy swings.
2. Competing for the "China plus one" supply chain shift. As global manufacturers look to diversify sourcing away from China, FTAs that lower tariffs and simplify rules of origin make India a more credible alternative manufacturing and export base, especially in textiles, engineering goods, pharmaceuticals and electronics.
3. Domestic political economy — "Atmanirbhar Bharat" meets market access. Indian negotiators have been explicit that every agreement in this cycle protects "sensitive" sectors - dairy, agriculture, and select domestic industries, while opening up manufacturing and services exports. This reflects a calculated balance: liberalise where India has comparative advantage (textiles, leather, engineering goods, IT/ITES, professional mobility) while shielding sensitive rural constituencies. The government has tied the entire push to its longer-term "Viksit Bharat @2047" (Developed India by 2047) ambition.
An analytical view: gains, gaps, and the fine print
The headline trade and GDP figures - tens of billions of dollars in additional bilateral trade, single-digit-billion-pound GDP contributions from the UK deal alone are meaningful but need to be read with some caution:
* These are long-run modelled estimates, not guarantees. The UK government's own £5.1 billion GDP estimate for India is explicitly a 2040 projection relative to a "no agreement" counterfactual, not an annual certainty. Realisation depends on how many exporters actually claim preferential tariffs (utilisation rates), whether firms can meet rules-of-origin requirements, and how quickly customs and certification systems adapt - India's Certificate of Origin issuances rose from about 685,000 in FY2023-24 to roughly 721,000 in FY2024-25, showing rising but still partial uptake of existing FTA preferences.
* Sectoral winners are clearer than aggregate ones. Labour-intensive, employment-heavy sectors - textiles and apparel, leather and footwear, gems and jewellery, marine products, engineering goods stand to gain the most tangible, near-term benefit from tariff elimination in the UK, EU, Oman and New Zealand markets. Sectors like Scotch whisky and automobiles illustrate the flip side: India is opening its own market meaningfully (UK whisky tariffs falling from 150% toward 40% over a decade, auto tariffs cut sharply), which will pressure some domestic producers even as it lowers costs for consumers.
* The EU deal is the biggest wildcard. It is the most consequential but execution intensive. Beyond tariff reductions, its impact will hinge on compliance with stringent EU standards on SPS, carbon, data and IP. With ratification and implementation likely to take time, the economic benefits are expected to materialise gradually rather than immediately.
* The US relationship remains unresolved. A framework for an "interim" arrangement is not a comprehensive FTA, and tariff overhang from 2025 US actions continues to be a swing factor in India's export outlook, arguably a bigger near-term risk to GDP than any of the completed deals are an upside.
What this means for India's GDP trajectory
All the official forecasters (IMF, World Bank and RBI) have trimmed FY27 estimates over the past few months, converging around 6.4–6.6%, driven by the energy shock, not the trade agenda. The consistent thread across these projections is that India remains the fastest-growing major economy in the world, but the FTA wave is best understood as a structural tailwind rather than a near-term growth trigger. Trade agreements typically take several years to show up meaningfully in export and investment data, what they do more immediately is reduce policy uncertainty, diversify India's trade base away from any single large partner, and signal to global manufacturers and investors that India is opening up on its own terms rather than under external pressure.
The bottom line
India's twelve-month FTA sprint — UK, EFTA, Oman, New Zealand, and the long-awaited EU deal, alongside a US framework and new GCC and EAEU negotiations reflects a structural shift in India’s trade approach, from defensive trade policy to actively and aggressively securing market access, diversifying trade relationships and embedding India deeper into global value chains. India is quietly shifting from just being a large consumer market to becoming a global trade rule-shaper, with FTAs serving as tools for influence, investment attraction and supply-chain positioning rather than sheer export growth. Over time, India could gain influence over emerging trade standards in areas such as digital trade, sustainability, supply-chain resilience and professional mobility.
The real outcome of India's FTA sprint may not be more trade alone. It may be India's emergence as one of the few economies that helps shape how global trade gets positioned over the next decade.
The economic upside is real but back-loaded: the tangible near-term impact is risk management (reducing dependence on any single market amid global tariff volatility) and positioning India as a credible alternative manufacturing and export hub. Whether the GDP arithmetic in official projections materialises will depend less on the signatures already inked and more on implementation, ratification timelines, exporters' ability to actually use the preferences on offer, and whether the still-unresolved pieces, especially with the United States, get finalised in the way India's trade negotiators are hoping for.

articles.title: Rubio, Jaishankar hold talks as US, India seek to finalise trade deal - United News of Bangladesh

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio held talks with Indian Foreign Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar in Mumbai on Tuesday as Washington and New Delhi seek to finalise a long-delayed trade agreement and strengthen energy cooperation.
The two countries are trying to revive trade negotiations that stalled for months amid tensions over US tariffs and India's purchases of Russian oil.
“We’re very, very close. I would say we’re about as close as you can be without having executed the agreement,” Rubio told reporters in Mumbai, adding that only a small number of issues remained to be resolved and an agreement could be reached shortly.
India's foreign ministry said the discussions were expected to cover major areas of bilateral cooperation, including energy, trade, investment and defence.
Washington imposed tariffs of up to 50% on most Indian goods in August 2025 after trade negotiations broke down. Under a framework agreed in February 2026, the tariff rate was reduced to 18%, but talks have since made little progress.
Earlier this month, Indian Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman said the negotiations had “plateaued”. However, Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal said last week that the first phase of a trade agreement was in its final stages.
India wants its final tariff rate to be comparable to those imposed on competing manufacturing economies such as Vietnam.
Energy trade has also been a source of friction between the two countries. India's purchases of discounted Russian crude since the start of the war in Ukraine have periodically strained relations with Washington.
New Delhi has said it plans to expand energy imports, including from the United States, while diversifying its suppliers to maintain market stability and keep prices affordable.
Speaking to reporters on Saturday before leaving for India, Rubio acknowledged that New Delhi had diversified its energy sources but continued to import substantial quantities of Russian oil, making an immediate shift to other suppliers difficult.
“You’ve got countries like India, for example, that have voluntarily diversified their energy portfolio but are still getting a substantial amount of energy from Russia because it’s hard to pivot from one day to the next,” he said, describing India as an important US ally and partner.
Despite disagreements over trade and energy, Washington and New Delhi continue to strengthen cooperation in defence and technology. The United States considers India an important strategic counterweight to China in the Indo-Pacific region.
Rubio's visit to India followed a trip to Uzbekistan aimed at promoting trade and strengthening ties with Central Asian countries.
According to the US State Department, Rubio is scheduled to visit a refinery in Jamnagar, Gujarat, on Wednesday and meet business leaders.
The facility, operated by Indian billionaire Mukesh Ambani's Reliance Industries, is the world's largest refining complex. In March, US President Donald Trump announced that the company was investing $300 billion to establish an oil refinery in Brownsville, Texas.

- The shutdown threatens export earnings and traders’ livelihoods, with no confirmed date for trade to resume.
Pakistan has suspended commercial trade through two key crossings with Iran, leaving about 2,000 trucks stranded on both sides of the border, according to the Quetta Chamber of Commerce and Industry (QCCI). The vehicles are carrying goods including liquefied petroleum gas (LPG), rice and fresh fruit, raising concerns over supply disruptions and losses for traders.
The suspension emerged on Saturday, October 17, after Pakistan’s Ministry of Commerce withdrew an earlier order concerning imports from Iran. Pakistani officials have cited security concerns, smuggling and border management, while Tehran has attributed the disruption to technical issues and precautionary measures. Neither government has announced a confirmed reopening date in the reports reviewed. The closure comes as Islamabad seeks to maintain relations with Tehran amid wider regional tensions and diplomatic efforts to prevent further conflict.
Why Did Pakistan Suspend Trade At The Two Crossings?
The precise administrative trigger for the suspension remains unclear. On October 16, Pakistan’s Ministry of Commerce issued a memorandum withdrawing an earlier order dated October 3 concerning an extension of the Electronic Import Form (EIF) waiver for imports from Iran. The memorandum did not specify why the earlier order was withdrawn, and the available reporting does not establish whether the decision directly caused the suspension of commercial trade.
Balochistan officials subsequently cited security and border management concerns. Shahid Rind, adviser to the provincial chief minister on media and political affairs, described the move as “necessary to improve the security situation and administrative affairs on both sides of the border”, India Today reported. Al Jazeera reported that Pakistan’s federal government had not publicly commented on the suspension.
Bakhtiar Ismail, deputy commissioner of Chagai district, where Taftan is located, said the measure was temporary. “The border will be opened as soon as effective measures are in place,” he wrote on X, according to Al Jazeera.
Iran offered a different explanation. Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said: “Due to certain technical issues and the necessity of implementing precautionary measures, cross-border movement and exchanges have been temporarily halted,” according to the state-run IRNA news agency.
Pakistan’s security explanation and Iran’s account of technical problems have not been reconciled publicly. The available reporting does not establish whether the withdrawal of the import waiver directly triggered the suspension or whether separate operational decisions were involved.
The reported suspension concerns commercial trade through Taftan and Gabd-Rimdan. The QCCI said commercial activity had been suspended across all Pakistan-Iran border crossings, although the reported government action specifically names the two crossings.
What Goods Are Stranded And Who Could Be Affected?
The stranded vehicles are carrying LPG, rice, fresh fruit and other essential commodities, according to PTI.
The chamber has advised businesses trading with Iran to stop placing fresh import and export orders until further notice. Traders now face uncertainty over delivery schedules, customs clearance and the costs of consignments that cannot move. Transporters may also incur additional expenses while vehicles and cargo remain stranded.
Gabd-Rimdan is an important route for Pakistan’s LPG supplies. The suspension has raised concerns about possible disruptions to availability and upward pressure on prices, although the scale of any shortage or price increase has not been established. The impact will depend on how long the restrictions last and whether alternative supplies are available.
The disruption could also affect Pakistani rice exporters. UN trade data available through the World Bank put Pakistan’s rice exports to Iran at about $430.5 million in 2023, underlining the importance of the market for exporters, Arab News reported. Muhammad Raza, chairman of the Rice Exporters Association of Pakistan, told Arab News that redirecting shipments through Iran’s Bandar Abbas port would be difficult because of higher freight costs amid the US-Iran conflict.
“To divert all to Bandar Abbas [port in Iran] would be very difficult as due to the [US-Iran] war the cost of freight is very high,” Raza said.
Fresh produce is particularly vulnerable to delays because it can deteriorate while awaiting clearance. Border communities could also face reduced work for drivers, loaders, customs clearing agents, warehouse workers and small businesses providing transport and related services. These are potential consequences; the reports reviewed do not establish the extent of actual job losses or financial damage.
The closure has not halted all movement. Iran’s WANA news agency reported that passenger traffic through the Rimdan-Gabd crossing continued even as commercial operations were suspended. The restrictions therefore concern commercial movement rather than necessarily preventing all travel across the border.
Security Concerns And The Wider Regional Context
The suspension comes against a backdrop of prolonged insecurity in Balochistan, where armed groups have carried out attacks on security personnel and government installations. Pakistani authorities have sought to strengthen security in the province, which shares a border with Iran’s Sistan and Baluchestan region.
However, the available reporting does not establish that a specific attack directly triggered the current suspension. Pakistani officials have cited broader security and counterterrorism concerns, but the precise operational circumstances behind the closure remain unclear.
The decision also comes amid tensions involving Iran, the United States and Israel. Pakistan has sought to mediate between Washington and Tehran and has been involved in diplomatic efforts to prevent further escalation.
In January 2024, Iran launched strikes inside Pakistan’s Balochistan province, prompting retaliatory Pakistani strikes inside Iran two days later. Subsequent diplomatic engagement helped ease the immediate crisis. The episode illustrates how security disputes along the shared frontier can strain relations, although there is no evidence that the current trade suspension has triggered a comparable confrontation.
The timing is significant for Islamabad’s diplomatic efforts. Reuters that Pakistan’s army chief, Field Marshal Asim Munir, was scheduled to visit Tehran on October 20 for talks with Iranian officials amid efforts to revive negotiations between Washington and Tehran. Arab News reported that discussions were also likely to cover bilateral relations and measures to facilitate trade along the shared border. The visit provides a diplomatic channel for addressing the disruption, although available reporting does not establish that reopening the crossings was its primary purpose.
Javad Heiran-Nia, head of the Persian Gulf Studies Group at Iran’s Center for Scientific Research and Middle East Strategic Studies, warned that an unresolved dispute could complicate Pakistan’s diplomatic position.
“If the border dispute remains unresolved, Tehran may question whether Islamabad can simultaneously maintain productive relations with Iran and cooperate with Washington’s pressure campaign,” he told Al Jazeera.
His assessment highlights a possible diplomatic risk, rather than evidence that relations have already deteriorated because of the suspension.
What Have Pakistan And Iran Said About Reopening The Crossings?
Pakistani officials have described the closure as temporary and said discussions are under way to resolve the outstanding issues. Rind expressed the expectation that trade would resume soon, while Ismail said the border would reopen once effective measures were in place.
Baghaei also said Iranian and Pakistani authorities were in contact to resolve the technical problems and restore normal operations. Neither side has announced a confirmed reopening date in the reports reviewed.
The immediate challenge is to agree on the security and administrative arrangements needed to resume trade, including the clearance of stranded consignments and the procedures for new orders. Pakistan must address its stated security concerns without prolonging disruptions to legitimate commerce, while Iran must work with Pakistani authorities to resolve the technical issues it has cited.
A prolonged suspension could increase transport costs and expose traders to losses while disrupting supplies. Neither government had announced a confirmed reopening date in the reports reviewed. The outcome of their discussions will determine how quickly commercial movement can resume.
