PRNewswire
New Delhi [India], October 20: The global race to build infrastructure for artificial intelligence is giving world trade strong momentum at a time of higher tariffs and geopolitical conflicts.
- The AI boom has become a powerful driver of global trade - outweighing tariffs and geopolitical shocks, according to the latest DHL Globalization Tracker
- The trade outlook has improved, with growth through 2029 now forecast to outpace the previous decade
- South and Central Asia to have the second-fastest goods-trade growth over 2026-29, behind only the Middle East & North Africa
- India continues to strengthen its trade resiliency by developing new trade agreements
- Globalization has reached a record level of 25.8%
This is one of the key findings of the latest edition of the DHL Globalization Tracker, released by DHL and New York University's Stern School of Business. Based on more than 30 million data points, the report analyzes international flows of trade, capital, information, and people. It offers the most comprehensive view of globalization available. This edition marks the report's first publication under its new name. It was previously known as the 'DHL Global Connectedness Tracker'.
AI buildout boosts global trade
The report shows that global goods trade grew faster in the first half of 2026 than in any half-year in the past 15 years, apart from the exceptional Covid rebound. A major driver was strong demand for goods used to build AI infrastructure, such as semiconductors and data-transmission equipment. Trade in AI-enabling goods drove 42% of goods trade growth in 2025, and this share rose to 76% during the first quarter of 2026, according to WTO and OECD analysis.
'The biggest story in global trade right now is AI - not tariffs,' said John Pearson, CEO of DHL Express. 'Every AI query ultimately depends on logistics. Chips, networking equipment and the many other goods behind this technology must be in the right place at the right time. DHL connects the businesses and markets behind these complex supply chains. Whenever innovation creates new trade flows, our global network helps keep them moving.'
Global effects of Iran war and tariffs remain limited
At the same time, the Iran war and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz disrupted important trade routes. But the effects remained concentrated. Economies dependent on the Strait were hit particularly hard. For example, the value of trade fell 37% in Saudi Arabia and 7% in the United Arab Emirates in the first five months of 2026 compared with the same period in 2025.
Trade policy created a separate headwind. U.S. tariffs reached their highest levels in decades, but their global impact was limited. One reason is that the U.S. accounted for only 13% of world imports in recent years, with roughly half of those imports exempt from the tariff increases as of August 2026. Another is that most countries refrained from broad retaliation. Many instead increased efforts to secure access to alternative markets through new trade agreements.
Trade outlook upgraded despite recent shocks
Looking ahead, global goods trade is projected to expand by an average of 3.4% per year through 2029. That would be substantially faster than the 2.7% rate recorded over the previous decade.
'The surprise is not only that global trade kept growing through new tariffs and the Iran war,' said Prof. Steven A. Altman, Director of the DHL Initiative on Globalization at NYU Stern's Center for the Future of Management. 'The outlook is now stronger than it was before either shock. This reminds us to look beyond the most visible disruptions and recognize the deeper reasons why trade remains so resilient. The AI trade boom highlights the demand for goods and services that can only be provided efficiently when specialized producers work together across countries. It also shows how companies continually adapt to keep trade moving through disruptions and policy shifts.'
India sits within one of the world's strongest trade-growth regions, East Asia and the Pacific leads the way in 2026
Among all regions, East Asia and the Pacific recorded the strongest trade growth. The value of its trade rose 24% in the first five months of 2026 compared with the same period in 2025. Europe followed with 12% and Sub-Saharan Africa with 11%. South and Central Asia recorded a trade value growth of 9.6%. Looking forward, the region's forecast remain the second-fastest for goods-trade growth over 2026-29, behind only the Middle East and North Africa.
East Asia and the Pacific not only recorded the strongest growth, but also saw a larger share of its trade stay within the region. This share increased from 57% in 2025 to 60% in the first five months of 2026. Strong Asian supply chains serving the AI boom contributed to this increase.
India focuses on market diversification
One of the major changes in international flows is the weakening of U.S.-China ties. Yet the global impact remains surprisingly small. For example, trade between the U.S. and China accounted for 3.5% of world trade at its peak in 2015, before falling to only 1.6% during the first five months of 2026. The U.S.-China share of international business investment is even smaller - less than 1%. Meanwhile, close U.S. allies have largely maintained their relationships with China. These findings challenge the idea that U.S.-China decoupling is dividing the world economy into rival blocs.
A closer look also shows that direct trade figures understate U.S. reliance on China. Goods imported into the U.S. from other countries contain growing amounts of Chinese materials and components. When these indirect imports are also taken into account, U.S. reliance on China has declined only slightly through 2024, the latest year for which data are available.
While U.S.-China ties are weakening, India's trade relationship with the U.S. remains strong. At the same time, trade resilience remains a focus as India continues to expand its trade relationships, developing trade agreements with the European Union, the United Kingdom, the European Free Trade Association, New Zealand, and Oman.
Globalization reaches a new record
Beyond trade and investment patterns, the report tracks the broader development of globalization based on international flows of trade, capital, information and people. It uses a scale from 0% (no cross-border flows) to 100% (borders and distance have no impact). In 2025, globalization reached a record level of 25.8%, supported in part by AI-related trade and investment.
All four flow categories contributed to the new record, reaching higher levels of internationalization. Information flows remain the most globalized, followed by capital and trade flows. People flows remain the least globalized.
The DHL Globalization Tracker
The DHL Globalization Tracker is a concise report and interactive website that provides regular updates on globalization and global trade. It complements the renowned DHL Globalization Report, published regularly since 2011. Drawn from over 25 public, private, and academic sources, the Tracker analyzes more than 30 million data points on international flows of trade, capital, information, and people.It includes interactive online charts that make it easy for users to explore trends by region, geopolitical alignment, and for individual countries. It also supports easy data and chart downloads for offline use.
The DHL Globalization Tracker is commissioned by DHL and authored by Prof. Steven A. Altman and Caroline R. Bastian of New York University Stern School of Business. It is available, together with further resources, at dhl.com/globalization.
Note: The DHL Globalization Tracker and DHL Globalization Report were formerly known as the 'DHL Global Connectedness Tracker' and 'DHL Global Connectedness Report'. Their new names more directly reflect the focus of the research. The scope and underlying approach remain unchanged, ensuring continuity with previous editions.
At a glance: The October 2026 edition of the DHL Globalization Tracker
What is the main finding of the report?
The global boom in artificial intelligence is giving world trade strong momentum despite higher tariffs and geopolitical conflicts. Global goods trade grew faster in the first half of 2026 than in any half-year in the past 15 years, apart from the exceptional Covid rebound.
Beyond trade, the report tracks the broader development of globalization based on international flows of trade, capital, information and people. In 2025, globalization reached a record level of 25.8%. The report measures this using a scale from 0% (no cross-border flows) to 100% (borders and distance have no impact). All four types of flows contributed to the record, becoming more international.
What is the outlook for global trade?
The outlook has improved. Global goods trade is projected to grow by an average of 3.4% per year through 2029. That would be significantly faster than the 2.7% annual growth rate recorded over the previous decade. Notably, current forecasts are more optimistic than those made before both the 2025-26 U.S. tariff increases and the Iran war, suggesting that recent shocks have had a smaller impact on the global economy than many expected.
How have tariffs and geopolitical conflicts affected global trade?
Tariffs and geopolitical conflicts continue to create risks and disruptions. But their overall impact on global trade has been limited. While the Iran war affected important shipping routes and hit economies dependent on the Strait of Hormuz particularly hard, the effects remained largely concentrated. U.S. tariffs rose to their highest levels in decades, but the United States accounted for only 13% of world imports in recent years, and roughly half of U.S. imports were exempt from tariff increases as of August 2026. Many countries also avoided broad retaliation and instead expanded trade links with alternative markets. As a result, global trade continued to grow.

articles.title: From Nepal, Sri Lanka to Bangladesh: How mass political protests left nations broken - Organiser
articles.summary: From Nepal, Sri Lanka to Bangladesh: How mass political protests left nations broken  Organiser
articles.full_text:
Mass protests are often presented as a means of bringing political change and demanding accountability. However, their economic consequences can extend well beyond the immediate political crisis. Prolonged agitation, disruption of public services and institutional instability can leave ordinary citizens struggling with lost income, rising prices and fewer employment opportunities.
Drawing on the experiences of Sri Lanka, Bangladesh and Nepal against treating political upheaval as a guaranteed path to democratic or economic improvement. The costs of instability are often borne by workers, small traders, daily-wage earners and middle-class households, even after the immediate political confrontation has ended.
Sri Lanka, Bangladesh and Nepal: Lessons from unrest
Sri Lanka’s Aragalaya movement culminated in the departure of President Gotabaya Rajapaksa in 2022, amid a severe economic crisis. Although the country has since made progress towards macroeconomic recovery under an International Monetary Fund-supported programme, the commentary points to continuing poverty and household financial pressures as reminders of the crisis’s long-term impact.
In Bangladesh, student-led protests over government job quotas in 2024 expanded into a wider anti-government movement that led to the fall of Sheikh Hasina’s government. Nalawade argues that the political transition did not automatically resolve the country’s economic difficulties, with inflation, industrial disruption and employment concerns continuing to affect ordinary people.
Nepal’s political turbulence has also be to put into question whether changes in government necessarily translate into lasting institutional or economic reform. Political leaders and influential groups can often adapt to changing circumstances, while citizens remain exposed to uncertainty and economic hardship.
Ordinary citizens bear the cost
There is vulnerability among people whose livelihoods depend on the uninterrupted movement of goods, functioning markets and stable employment. Prolonged road blockades can affect truck drivers and transport workers, while market closures and industrial disruptions can hurt small businesses, vendors and wage earners.
Economic instability can also reduce household purchasing power. When prices rise faster than wages, families face greater difficulty meeting basic expenses. For middle-class households, inflation can erode savings, while workers in vulnerable sectors may face reduced hours or job losses.
The political organisers and influential figures may be better placed to withstand these disruptions than the people who participate in, or are affected by, prolonged unrest.
India’s warning against prolonged disruption
Notably, India could face serious economic consequences if political mobilisation develops into sustained disruption of institutions, manufacturing centres and transport networks. It argues that political campaigns framed around constitutional protection and accountability should also be judged by their methods and their potential consequences for the wider public.
It is important to ask whether calls for nationwide agitation adequately account for the impact on small businesses, daily-wage workers, supply chains and investor confidence. It urges citizens to consider the economic consequences of prolonged unrest alongside the political demands being advanced.
The central argument is that democratic accountability and political reform should not be confused with disorder. Notably, India’s long-term strength depends on preserving institutional stability while allowing democratic debate and peaceful protest.

A photo showing a couple at the Masjid al-Haram in Saudi Arabia's Mecca is being widely shared on social media, claiming that it shows a Bangladeshi man and woman who were executed for carrying out 'indecent acts' at the holy site.
The claim: Those sharing the image, including Supreme Court lawyer Shashank Shekhar Jha, have shared it with text which says, "Saudi Arabia has EXECUTED Newlywed Bangladeshi Couple Nazrul Islam Abdul Basir and Siri Akhtar. Nazrul merely “Kissed his Pregnant Wife's Belly” inside Mecca Mosque (sic)."
- While Saudi Arabia executed two Bangladeshi nationals for 'indecent acts' at the holy site, it neither mentioned the nature of the act, nor did they specify the manner of execution.
How did we find out the truth?: We set out to verify whether a newlywed Bangladeshi couple had been executed after the husband kissed his wife's pregnant belly at the Kaaba.
- A relevant keyword search led us to a report by the BBC, which confirmed that a man and a woman from Bangladesh had been executed, but there were no specific details about their relationship or the nature of the act.
- Bangladeshi news organisation Jago News 24 spoke to the deceased man's father, who stated that the woman was not his son's wife and that they did not know her.
- When then checked the website of the Saudi Press Agency (SPA), which published all official communication from the Kingdom.
- Dated 14 October 2026, a release on this website mentioned that two Bangladeshi nationals, a man and a woman, identified as "Nadhir Al Islam Abdul Basir and Siti Akhtar," were sentenced to death after the "committed an indecent act inside one of the mosques in the Holy City."
Evidently, there is no explicit mention of the act itself, the relationship between the man and the woman, or the manner of execution.
What about the photo?: A reverse image search on the viral photo led us to a Facebook post shared on 24 December 2024, which carried the photo in question.
- It mentioned that it showed "blogger Jihad Al-Banna and her husband's pregnancy photoshoot (sic)" in front of the Kaaba.
- Taking a cue from this, we looked for the woman's social media account, which helped us identify her as Gehad Elbana, an Egyptian influencer.
- Elbana had shared images similar to the one in the viral claim on her Instagram account on 23 December 2024, announcing her pregnancy in a post which had also tagged her husband.
Conclusion: An old photo of a couple is being falsely linked to the recent execution of a Bangladeshi man and woman in Saudi Arabia.

What the Justice department said banning Cloudera from PERM
In the official release, DOJ said:
“The U.S. Department of Justice’s Civil Rights Division (CRT) and the U.S. Department of Labor (DOL) today announced a coordinated enforcement resolution with Cloudera Inc., a Santa Clara, California-based data management company, following allegations that the company discriminated against qualified U.S. workers during recruitment conducted under the Permanent Labor Certification (PERM) program.
“There are no exceptions: the Justice Department will hold accountable employers who discriminate against U.S. workers,” said Assistant Attorney General Harmeet K. Dhillon of the Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division. “This substantial settlement, in partnership with DOL, sends a strong signal to employers that the federal government will work together to ensure employers treat U.S. workers fairly.”
As part of the resolution, Cloudera will be barred from participating in the PERM program for two years, one of the most significant sanctions available for DOL to protect the integrity of the employment-based immigration system and safeguard opportunities for U.S. workers. The debarment follows DOL’s earlier suspension of Cloudera’s PERM processing and reflects DOL’s commitment to aggressively enforcing labor certification requirements when employers fail to provide U.S. workers a fair opportunity to compete for jobs.
The settlement also resolves a lawsuit DOJ filed in April of this year, alleging that Cloudera violated the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA) by discriminating against U.S. workers when recruiting and hiring for seven positions under the PERM process. Under the terms of the settlement with the Justice Department, Cloudera will establish a back-pay fund of $1.4 million to compensate qualified U.S. workers who tried to apply for the jobs at issue but were not given fair consideration. Cloudera also will pay $600,000 in civil penalties to the United States.

Saudi Arabia postponed its flagship Future Investment Initiative (FII) conference as the Houthis claimed fresh attacks across the kingdom. The delay underscores mounting security concerns and disruption to the Gulf's business calendar.
Saudi Arabia has postponed its flagship Future Investment Initiative (FII), informally known as "Davos in the Desert", conference until 2027 amid escalating tensions in the Middle East, as Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi rebels claimed fresh attacks on oil facilities, airports and military targets across the kingdom.
The organisers confirmed the postponement in a statement on Monday, saying the 10th edition of the high-profile investment conference, originally scheduled for October 26 to 29, would now take place next year. A new date will be announced "very soon".
HOUTHIS CLAIM STRIKES ON SAUDI OIL FACILITIES, AIRPORTS
The Houthis said they had carried out several attacks on Saudi targets, including an Aramco facility in Yanbu, the Shaybah oilfield, King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh and Abha airport.
There was no immediate confirmation from Saudi Arabia, and Reuters could not independently verify the claims.
The kingdom has faced escalating attacks in recent weeks, with strikes targeting military installations, energy infrastructure and civilian facilities. Attacks this month reportedly hit Aramco's headquarters and Riyadh's international airport, killing at least 18 people and leaving hundreds wounded, according to the report.
SAUDI ARABIA DELAYS FLAGSHIP INVESTMENT SUMMIT UNTIL 2027
The postponement comes as the conflict involving the US, Israel and Iran widens across the region, disrupting business activities and raising security concerns.
The FII conference, now in its 10th edition, has become a major gathering for global financiers, business leaders and policymakers. Informally known as "Davos in the Desert", the state-backed event showcases Saudi Arabia's investment ambitions as it seeks to diversify its economy away from hydrocarbons and expand sectors such as tourism, sports and technology.
This year's expected speakers included Goldman Sachs CEO and Chairman David Solomon, Standard Chartered CEO Bill Winters and Citi CEO Jane Fraser, according to a draft programme.
MIDDLE EAST WAR DISRUPTS GULF'S BUSINESS CALENDAR
The conflict has already disrupted the Gulf's busy calendar of business events, with several conferences cancelled, postponed or restructured in the United Arab Emirates and Qatar earlier this year as the countries came under attack.
FII organisers said the postponement was intended to ensure that the event delivered "the full scale, extraordinary quality, and unforgettable impact" expected by its global community.
SECURITY CONCERNS RAISED OVER SUMMIT ATTENDANCE
Reuters reported last week that the organisers had considered a hybrid format that would allow executives to participate remotely.
Meanwhile, Semafor reported on Monday that major banks and private-equity firms had privately conveyed security concerns about attending the conference to Saudi Public Investment Fund Governor Yasir Al-Rumayyan. The report added that chief executives felt pressure to attend the four-day event.
The postponement marks a setback for Saudi Arabia's efforts to position itself as a global investment hub and attract international capital to support its economic transformation.

articles.summary: Why are India and the US still waiting to announce a trade deal?  India Today
articles.full_text:
Marco Rubio said India and the US were close to finalising a trade agreement. Market access differences and shifting tariff rules raise questions about its durability.
For months, senior officials in India and the United States have said a trade deal is close. On Tuesday, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio repeated that message in Mumbai, saying the two sides were “about as close as you can be without having an executed agreement."
So what is holding up the announcement?
Differences over market access remain. But Washington’s shifting tariff policy raises another question: how reliable will the terms negotiated today be tomorrow?
THE QUESTION IS TARIFF CERTAINTY
Under President Donald Trump, the United States has justified tariffs on grounds ranging from national security and fentanyl trafficking to economic emergencies and allegedly unfair trade practices.
Tariffs themselves are not unusual. Countries use them to protect domestic industries and seek concessions from trading partners. The difficulty arises when the legal basis, scope and duration of those duties keep changing.
A tariff imposed under one law may be challenged in court, while another provision allows Washington to introduce a different duty. For businesses and negotiating partners, that makes future trading conditions harder to predict.
A long-term agreement requires confidence that negotiated benefits will last.
DIFFERENT LAWS, DIFFERENT LIMITS
Under the US Constitution, Congress has the power to impose tariffs and regulate foreign trade. It has delegated specific powers to the president through laws designed for different circumstances.
The Trump administration has drawn on several of these authorities:
- International Emergency Economic Powers Act, 1977: Used for the sweeping “Liberation Day” reciprocal tariffs and certain fentanyl-related duties. On February 20, 2026, the Supreme Court ruled that the law did not authorise presidential tariffs.
- Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act, 1962: Used to impose tariffs on products such as steel, aluminium and automobiles on national-security grounds.
- Section 301 of the Trade Act, 1974: Provides authority to act against specified unfair foreign trade practices, subject to an investigation and statutory procedures.
- Section 122 of the Trade Act, 1974: Invoked after the Supreme Court ruling to impose a temporary, broad import surcharge to address balance-of-payments problems. Such measures cannot continue beyond 150 days without congressional action.
These powers are not interchangeable. Each has its own conditions, procedures and limits. Moving from one authority to another does not remove those requirements or shield a tariff from legal challenge.
The issue is therefore not an absence of American tariff laws. It is how the administration uses overlapping powers, and how much certainty a negotiated agreement can provide against future duties.
WHAT THIS MEANS FOR INDIA
A trade deal could lower tariffs on agreed goods. But depending on its terms and applicable US law, separate national-security or unfair-trade duties could still affect those products.
For Indian exporters, the question is whether the agreement would deliver lasting market access. For businesses considering new factories, supply chains or export contracts, that certainty affects investment decisions.
This creates an additional negotiating challenge: securing a favourable tariff today may not be enough if other duties can alter the commercial terms later.
That does not establish tariff uncertainty as the reason the announcement has been delayed. Without confirmation from negotiators, it is better understood as a risk to the durability of a deal.
TARIFFS ARE NOT THE ONLY HURDLE
India and the US also have longstanding differences over agricultural and dairy market access, industrial tariffs, digital trade, intellectual property and regulatory standards.
Washington wants greater access for American businesses. New Delhi must weigh those demands against domestic producers’ interests and its own policy priorities.
Those disagreements would exist under a different US administration too. They require compromises over what each side opens, what it protects and how quickly changes take effect.
The tariff dispute adds another layer: whether concessions made by either side will produce predictable benefits.
WHAT WOULD MAKE A DEAL LAST?
India wants reliable access to the American market. The US wants fewer barriers to sell goods and services in India.
An agreement must bridge those demands while setting clear rules on tariff treatment, exceptions and disputes.
The challenge is therefore bigger than announcing a deal. It is ensuring that businesses can rely on it after the announcement.

What is worth watching next is whether the negotiating principals confirm the same timeline and whether any tariff-rate specifics or excluded sectors surface, since those are the details that have determined market follow-through in past episodes. - Marco Rubio said India and the US were close to concluding a trade agreement.
- He said only a small number of issues remained to be resolved.
- His remarks followed US waivers on sanctions linked to Russian energy purchases.
India and the United States are “very, very close” to concluding a trade agreement, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Tuesday, adding that only a few issues remained unresolved.
Rubio, on his second official visit to India, said he expected the agreement to be finalised shortly.
“The State Department doesn't negotiate trade agreements, but we are very much involved in what's happening...We're very, very close. I would say we're about as close as you can be without having executed the agreement. I think there's a small number of items left to wrap up, so I think that will happen shortly,” he said.
“So, we're very optimistic that we will have something in place here very soon,” Rubio added.
Trade Talks Amid Russian Energy Policy Shift
His comments followed Washington’s decision to waive some sanctions linked to Russia shortly before they were due to take effect. The measures would have targeted India, China and three other countries with tariffs of up to 100%.
Before the waiver, President Donald Trump announced an agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin to import Russian diesel to ease the impact of rising fuel prices in the US.
The decisions marked a shift from the administration’s earlier opposition to Russian energy purchases. Washington had cited India’s imports of Russian oil when imposing tariffs totalling 50% on Indian goods last year. Those duties were subsequently reduced to 18% as trade negotiations progressed.
Rubio said on Monday that efforts to conclude an agreement with India were among the considerations behind decisions on national security waivers.
'Smart Thing To Do To Diversify Energy Sources', Says Rubio
Asked in Mumbai about India’s purchases of Russian oil, Rubio welcomed its efforts to broaden its energy sources, describing diversification as a “smart thing to do”.
“I think what India has expressed repeatedly is its desire to diversify its energy portfolio, which is a smart thing to do. It's not easy to do that from one day to the next. I think they've made some substantial progress in that regard, and we're happy to see that,” he said.
During the visit, Rubio also met External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar for discussions on regional energy security.

The outcome of the talks could help clarify the direction of bilateral engagement and identify areas where the two governments can make progress despite their differences. However, the future of trade negotiations and the handling of energy-related concerns remain important issues for both sides.

Rubio is scheduled to arrive at Mumbai’s Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj International Airport at 2.15 pm on Tuesday, according to the Ministry of External Affairs (MEA). He will lay a wreath at the Taj memorial to honour the victims of the 26/11 terror attacks before holding bilateral talks with Jaishankar at the Taj Mahal Palace hotel.

Rubio will later attend the “Freedom 250 Reception” at the Jio World Convention Centre to mark the 250th anniversary of US independence. Jaishankar will be the guest of honour.
Trade deal and energy security in focus
The visit comes as both countries seek to advance negotiations on a proposed trade agreement amid friction over tariffs, energy imports and immigration policies.
Speaking in Uzbekistan ahead of his India visit, Rubio said the two sides were close to finalising the agreement.
"We're trying to finalise a trade deal with India right now. We're very close to doing that."
Rubio also linked the negotiations to Washington’s decision to grant a temporary waiver on certain sanctions related to Russian energy purchases. He said India’s energy requirements and its importance as a US partner were among the factors being considered.
"These sanctions were not just sanctions on Russia. They include tariffs on a number of countries—India, for example, and others. And so I think the president wants to take the 60-day period of time to sort of analyse what imposing both sanctions and tariffs will mean to the global economy and even to the U.S. economy," Rubio said.
He added that India had diversified its energy sources but continued to rely on Russian supplies because shifting to alternatives could not happen overnight.
"You've got countries like India, for example, that have voluntarily diversified their energy portfolio, but are still getting a substantial amount of energy from Russia because it's hard to pivot from one day to the next. But they're also an important ally and partner of the United States. So we need that period of time to sort of study all this and figure out what the right combination is," he added.

The proposed India base will build on the university's Partner-Enabled Learning model, creating opportunities for internships, work placements and international research collaboration
The University of Manchester has announced plans to establish a new center in Bengaluru, India, creating a permanent base for education, research and industry partnerships. The proposed development will bring the university's academic expertise together with Indian institutions and businesses, while expanding opportunities for students to gain practical experience with employers.
The announcement was made during the first Great North Mayoral Mission to India, held from 12 to 16 October 2026, which brought together universities, businesses, civic leaders and cultural organizations from across Northern England.
Bengaluru has been identified as the preferred location due to its concentration of universities, research institutions and technology businesses, including organizations already working with Manchester's academics and graduates.
New opportunities for students to work with industry
A central element of the proposed center is the expansion of the University of Manchester's Partner-Enabled Learning (PEL) model, which integrates employer-led projects and practical experience into degree programs.
Through the Bengaluru center, the university plans to create opportunities for internships, work placements and industry-led projects, connecting students with employers, public bodies and community organizations.
The existing PEL approach includes credit-bearing projects and micro-internships designed to develop skills such as problem-solving, adaptability and collaboration alongside academic study.
Manchester already has relationships with major Indian businesses, including Reliance, Tata and Infosys, as well as a wider network of technology companies. The proposed center will build on those connections to strengthen industry engagement and create further opportunities for students and researchers.
Manchester expands its research partnerships in India
The plans also extend an established network of academic partnerships between the university and Indian institutions.
In 2021, Manchester became the first UK university to establish a joint PhD program with an Indian institution, launching a dual-award arrangement with the Indian Institute of Technology Kharagpur (IIT Kharagpur).
Its other collaborations include the Indian Institute of Science Bangalore, BITS Pilani, Jawaharlal Nehru Centre for Advanced Scientific Research and Manipal Academy of Higher Education.
The proposed Bengaluru center will provide a permanent platform for further educational partnerships, collaborative research and innovation, connecting Manchester's academic expertise with India's research and technology communities.
Professor Duncan Ivison, President and Vice-Chancellor of the University of Manchester, says:
"There is an incredible depth to Manchester’s relationship with India across education, business and culture. Our new Centre will be at the heart of deepening those relationships and I’m very excited to see what we can give, and what we can learn over the coming years."
The announcement was made at an event at Science Gallery Bengaluru, attended by university alumni and leaders from business and culture. The program included panel discussions on innovation and culture led by Professor Ivison.
The proposed development forms part of the university's international strategy, From Manchester for the World, and its Manchester 2035 ambitions, which identify global engagement and international partnerships as institutional priorities.
Manchester already operates international centers in Dubai, Hong Kong, Shanghai and Singapore. Bengaluru would extend that network, although an opening date for the proposed center has not yet been announced.

New Delhi [India], October 20 (ANI): Violent anti-government protests in Albania, which saw demonstrators set fire to offices inside the Supreme Court in Tirana and target other government institutions, have triggered a political confrontation in India, with the BJP accusing Opposition leaders of encouraging 'anarchy and foreign-backed unrest', while Congress and other Opposition parties defended peaceful protests and rejected comparisons with violence overseas.
The political row intensified after Shiv Sena (UBT) MP Sanjay Raut referred to the unrest in Albania in a post on X, suggesting that countries, particularly India, should learn a lesson from the events.
His remarks drew criticism from BJP leaders and Union Minister Kiren Rijiju, while Opposition leaders, including Congress MPs Shashi Tharoor and Pawan Khera and Trinamool Congress MP Sougata Roy, pushed back against allegations that their protests were aimed at destabilising the government.
Amid the political exchange, Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) chief Mohan Bhagwat on Tuesday said that "regime change has neither happened nor will it happen", referring to protests in France and developments in Albania, Nepal and Bangladesh.
He stressed that demonstrations over social problems and shortcomings in the system were natural but must remain within constitutional and legal limits.
Addressing the Sangh's centenary-year Vijayadashami function at Reshimbagh ground in Nagpur, Bhagwat said protesters, the administration responsible for maintaining law and order, and political leaders must respect the Constitution, the law and the norms of civility in public life.
"Social participation and mutual dialogue must increase. We also have a responsibility to run society and the country," Bhagwat said.
He said protests arising from social problems were natural, but warned that when a demonstration had a different underlying purpose, it became political. He cautioned that such movements could deepen hostility and be exploited by forces opposed to the country.
Bhagwat urged political leaders to ensure that protests did not divide the country and society, emphasising that demonstrations must remain within constitutional limits. He also said society should not be caught in the grip of protests and that problems could not be easily resolved through movements alone.
In a post on X, Raut said, "The people of Albania have burned down the Supreme Court... helping corrupt prime ministers. The protesting public has also attacked the parliament and government offices... All countries should learn a lesson from these events. Especially India."
In another version of the remarks cited in the political exchange, Raut said the public was enraged because the Supreme Court was helping corrupt prime ministers, adding that protesters had also attacked ministers' homes.
The remarks led to a sharp response from Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) leader Pradeep Bhandari, who accused the Congress and its allies of threatening democratic institutions.
In a post on X, Bhandari said, "Congress party and its alliance are threatening anarchy and the Supreme Court! They are envisioning anarchy! This proves they want chaos! Congress party and its alliance are a threat to Indian Democracy!"
Union Minister Kiren Rijiju also alleged that attempts were being made to incite young people and spread violence in India, drawing parallels with unrest in France and Bangladesh. "Anti-India gangs and some politicians had colluded to incite the youth and spread violence on our streets," Rijiju said.
He further stated, "Regime change in India is absolutely possible, but only through elections, not through Soros."
The Union Minister's remarks reflected the ruling side's allegation that international networks and political actors were seeking to encourage unrest and undermine democratic institutions.
However, the Opposition rejected the allegations, maintaining that its protests over the Election Commission's Special Intensive Revision (SIR) exercise were intended to safeguard electoral rights and ensure free and fair elections.
Congress MP Shashi Tharoor rejected comparisons between India and countries witnessing violent unrest, asserting that the Opposition believed in peaceful demonstrations and constitutional methods. "India is not Bangladesh and India is not France... We only believe in peaceful protest," Tharoor said.
He added that the demand for free and fair elections was a constitutional issue and not an attempt to topple the government. "What we are calling for is free and fair elections. It's a constitutional issue, not an issue of trying to topple a regime," he said.
Congress MP Pawan Khera also criticised the ruling party's comparison of India with European countries, accusing it of using international developments to discredit peaceful protests. "Comparing India and Europe is comparing apples with oranges... They are recycling a tired, dangerous trope," Khera said.
He further alleged, "In Europe, the protesters are the rioters. In India, it is the State and state-sponsored non-state actors, the Sangh brigade."
The Opposition has raised concerns over the removal of names from electoral rolls during the SIR exercise, while the BJP has accused Opposition leaders of encouraging unrest. The exchange has further sharpened differences between the ruling party and Opposition over the objectives of protests in India.
Trinamool Congress MP Sougata Roy also responded to the controversy, making it clear that he did not support burning down a Supreme Court while defending the right to protest.
"We never support burning the Supreme Court anywhere, anytime, but it is justified for people to protest, and they are protesting in the country too. I do not support Sanjay Raut's statement," Roy said.
Uttar Pradesh Minister Om Prakash Rajbhar, meanwhile, condemned the attack on Albania's Supreme Court, stressing that the judiciary must be respected.
Reacting to Raut's post on X, Rajbhar said, "Certainly, this is a tragic event. Such things should not happen, and the judiciary is paramount. If the public has acted against the court in this manner, we condemn it. As for learning a lesson, people should indeed learn from such incidents."
Maharashtra Minister Gulabrao Patil also criticised Raut's remarks, accusing him of adopting contradictory positions on constitutional institutions. "On one hand, they talk about saving the Constitution, while on the other, they speak of burning down the Supreme Court. I believe their very intentions are flawed," Patil said.
He added, "Such theatrics will not work. The government here is strong. We will not allow their designs to succeed. The nation will not tolerate such rhetoric."
The developments in India stem from violent anti-government protests in Albania, where demonstrators have targeted government institutions and clashed with police while demanding the resignation of Prime Minister Edi Rama.
According to Al Jazeera, offices inside Albania's Supreme Court in the capital, Tirana, were set ablaze as the protests entered their fifth day on October 18. The unrest continued into a sixth consecutive day, with demonstrators also targeting parliament, ministry buildings and police forces.
Hundreds of protesters gathered again on Sunday outside the Ministry of Education, chanting "Rama, resign", amid a tense standoff with police. Security forces used rubber bullets, water cannons and tear gas to disperse or hold back the crowds.
The protests have been driven by demands for better education, more jobs, an end to alleged corruption and Rama's resignation. Local media reports cited by Al Jazeera said demonstrators were primarily targeting government institutions and police, including the Ministry of Education building and the area around Rama's office.
Shops and institutions in Tirana's city centre secured their doors and windows with metal shutters, while municipal workers removed paving stones to prevent protesters from using them during clashes.
According to a Ministry of Health report issued on Sunday morning, 65 people were injured, including 37 police officers, of whom 12 were hospitalised. Since Tuesday, 272 people had been injured in the clashes, including 169 police personnel.
Rama, who has been in office since 2013 and is serving his fourth term, has ruled out resigning and blamed a "foreign hand" for the unrest.
He has said that his government is doing its best to address corruption and is willing to listen to the "justified demands" of students and discuss the costs of education. However, he has insisted that those responsible for the destruction of property must be held accountable.
Discontent in Albania has been building for months. The first protests this year, dubbed the "Flamingo Revolution", began in May, when demonstrators opposed a controversial luxury tourist complex project in southern Albania reportedly affiliated with Jared Kushner, son-in-law of US President Donald Trump, Al Jazeera reported.
The unrest in Albania has become a flashpoint in India's domestic political debate, with the BJP accusing Opposition leaders of encouraging anarchy and invoking foreign-backed attempts at regime change, while Congress and other Opposition parties insist that their demands for electoral reforms and free and fair elections are rooted in constitutional principles. (ANI)

articles.title: 'Russia is a big machine': Trump says Ukraine 'has to want' to settle war with Putin - The Times of India
articles.summary: 'Russia is a big machine': Trump says Ukraine 'has to want' to settle war with Putin  The Times of India‘I don’t care how it’s done’: Trump pressures Ukraine to cut peace deal  Al JazeeraTrump Says Zelensky Should Get "Somebody Else" To Negotiate To End War  NDTVOpinion | Trump wants to make Zelenskyy his midterms scapegoat  MS NOWTrump’s Push for Deals With Russia Powers His Frustration With Ukraine  The New York Times
articles.full_text:
US President Donald Trump placed the burden on Ukraine to end the nearly four-year war with Russia, arguing that Moscow's military strength and territorial gains leave Kyiv at a disadvantage.
"Ukraine has to want to settle this war," Trump told reporters in the Oval Office, signalling that he expects Kyiv to move towards a negotiated settlement even as the fighting continues.
Trump pointed to Russia's ability to sustain its military campaign and capture territory, portraying Moscow as having the upper hand in the conflict.
"Russia is a big machine - they just keep grinding forward, and that's what they've done. They've taken a very large piece of land," he said.
His remarks came as his envoy Steve Witkoff held talks with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Oslo, Norway, on Tuesday as Washington continued its efforts to broker an end to Russia's invasion of Ukraine.
Trump also questioned the value of American assistance to Kyiv, complaining that Washington had spent heavily on supporting Ukraine without receiving anything in return.
"We've given a lot to Ukraine. We've gotten absolutely nothing back except grief, death, tremendous monetary loss," he said.
The US president also pointed to the deep hostility between Russian President Vladimir Putin and Zelenskyy, suggesting that their personal animosity had become an obstacle to negotiations. He described the hatred between the two leaders as "tremendous".
Trump further claimed that European countries were growing weary of the conflict, although European governments have been working to offset any reduction in American military support for Kyiv.
Trump eases sanctions pressure on Russia
Trump's push for a settlement comes as his administration has taken steps to ease economic pressure on Moscow, raising questions about whether the shift could strengthen Russia's position even as Washington seeks to end the war.
On Friday night, Trump signed an executive order exempting Russia from sanctions under a new measure passed by Congress last month. The decision provides additional economic relief to Moscow at a time when the US is also seeking Russian cooperation to bring down fuel prices.
The legislation, named after the late South Carolina Republican Senator Lindsey Graham, was designed to squeeze the financial resources sustaining Russia's war against Ukraine. It also gave Trump additional authority to impose tariffs on countries that continue to trade with Moscow.
The White House has broad powers to grant sanctions exemptions under the law. It requires the president to notify Congress if he decides against imposing the restrictions.
Trump exercised that authority two days before the sanctions were due to take effect.
“I am hereby waiving the application of such sanctions, restrictions and duties provided for in the Graham Act,” Trump said in the order. “I have submitted to the Congress a certification that the issuance of such a waiver at this time is in the national interests of the United States.”
The order did not explain in detail why lifting the restrictions would serve American interests or spell out the reasoning presented to Congress.
The decision marks another shift in Trump's approach to Russia. In recent weeks, he has expressed frustration with Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries, arguing that the strikes have contributed to rising petrol and diesel prices.
The administration has sought to ease fuel costs by allowing Russian diesel supplies into US and global markets, despite years of sanctions imposed on Moscow following its invasion of Ukraine.
However, the war involving Iran remains the biggest factor restricting fuel supplies, limiting how much relief the Russian measures can deliver.
US-Ukraine ties face growing strain
The sanctions waiver adds to mounting tensions between Washington and Kyiv, with Trump's latest remarks suggesting that his administration increasingly expects Ukraine to make concessions to end the conflict.
The relationship has also been affected by disruptions to satellite support for Ukrainian drones, raising concerns about Kyiv's ability to sustain its military operations if American assistance weakens further.
At the same time, Trump's decision to ease sanctions has drawn criticism from those who argue that reducing economic pressure could give Putin more resources to sustain the war rather than bring him closer to a settlement.
The administration's approach reflects its competing priorities. Trump wants to end the fighting, reduce economic pressures at home and limit the cost of continued American involvement. But his willingness to relax restrictions on Moscow has raised questions about the leverage Washington may be giving up in negotiations.
For Ukraine, the challenge is to secure an agreement that ends the fighting without sacrificing its territorial integrity or long-term security. Trump's latest comments make clear that he wants Kyiv to move towards a deal, while his assessment of Russia's battlefield advantage suggests he believes Ukraine has limited room to negotiate from strength.

articles.title: Nielsen Says India, With Bengaluru As Hub, Now Drives Its Global Innovation - IndiaWest
articles.summary: Nielsen Says India, With Bengaluru As Hub, Now Drives Its Global Innovation  IndiaWest
articles.full_text:
BENGALURU-US-based media analytics firm Nielsen is positioning India as its primary global innovation engine, with more than 5,000 employees in the country – roughly half its worldwide workforce – and Bengaluru serving as its largest hub, according to a report.
A report by Daily Sun, citing Moneycontrol, said around 75 per cent of Nielsen’s global innovation now comes from India, where the company has deployed artificial intelligence (AI) to automate advertising intelligence.
Nielsen Chief Technology Officer Anil Goel said AI helps automate the tracking of brand visibility in sports and measure audiences across an increasingly fragmented media landscape. The company aims to make India its “global innovation center” rather than operate it as a conventional global capability center (GCC).
“Unlike traditional GCCs where India-based teams work under overseas counterparts, Nielsen’s local teams lead products, make decisions and work directly with global clients,” the report said, citing Goel.
Although some other markets generate more revenue, Goel said India’s rapid growth makes it one of Nielsen’s top 10 markets in terms of growth potential.
Nielsen expects to expand its presence in India further following the addition of DoubleVerify, which specializes in advertising verification and brand safety. Goel also highlighted the country’s technology-heavy workforce as a factor creating more opportunities for the company to base innovation in India.
AI has made a significant impact on Nielsen’s advertising intelligence business, which tracks advertising expenditure across television, radio, newspapers, magazines and outdoor media in 30-40 major markets, including India and the US, the report said.
The company previously relied on a combination of automation and manual work to process information, with more than 1,000 employees handling gaps that technology could not resolve, according to the report. AI and large language models have increased the share of work handled by machines in these areas from 80-90 per cent to 97-98 per cent, Goel said.
The growing use of ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude, along with AI agents that help consumers make decisions, is creating new challenges for traditional methods of measuring media consumption, the report said. (IANS)

articles.title: Sergio Gor calls US and India ‘architects of the world of tomorrow’ at Mumbai reception - Business Upturn
articles.summary: Sergio Gor calls US and India ‘architects of the world of tomorrow’ at Mumbai reception  Business Upturn
articles.full_text:
US Ambassador to India Sergio Gor described the United States and India as “architects of the world of tomorrow” while highlighting cooperation in trade, technology, supply chains and Indo-Pacific security at the Freedom 250 reception in Mumbai on Tuesday. The event, held during US Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s visit to India, focused on the broader strategic and economic relationship between the two countries. The reception was scheduled at the Jio World Convention Centre.
Gor said the partnership was built not only in New Delhi and Washington but also across Indian cities, including Mumbai, Ahmedabad, Hyderabad, Chennai and Goa. He pointed to what he described as strong potential for deeper American engagement, linking the relationship to shared priorities in innovation, security and prosperity.
Trade and technology remain central priorities
The ambassador highlighted trade and resilient supply chains as important areas of cooperation. The emphasis comes as India and the United States seek to expand commercial ties while addressing differences over market access, tariffs and other economic issues.
Rubio’s visit provides an opportunity for officials from both countries to review their strategic partnership. India’s Ministry of External Affairs said ahead of the visit that discussions were expected to cover trade, energy, investment, defence, critical and emerging technologies, and regional and global developments.
Gor’s remarks also highlighted the role of Indian cities in shaping bilateral relations. His reference to multiple urban centres suggested that cooperation extends beyond government-level engagement to business, technology and other commercial opportunities across the country. However, the speech did not announce a new investment package, trade agreement or specific initiative involving the cities mentioned.
Quad and Indo-Pacific security
The ambassador also referred to a “free and open Indo-Pacific” and the Quad, the diplomatic grouping comprising India, the United States, Japan and Australia. The grouping works on regional cooperation, including maritime security, critical and emerging technologies, infrastructure and economic resilience.
For New Delhi and Washington, the Indo-Pacific remains an important area of strategic coordination as both countries pursue regional stability and stronger supply-chain networks. Gor’s comments reinforced the public emphasis on shared objectives, though they did not outline a new Quad commitment or policy change.
What comes next
The reception forms part of a wider series of engagements during Rubio’s India visit. His schedule includes discussions with External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar and a subsequent visit to Jamnagar, Gujarat, for engagements related to energy cooperation.
The next indicators of progress will be official readouts from the meetings and any concrete announcements on trade, investment, energy or defence. Gor’s remarks expressed confidence in the partnership, but the reception itself did not establish new agreements or implementation timelines.

articles.title: Britain sends Typhoon fighter jets to defend Saudi Arabia against Houthis, rules out offensive strikes - The Times of India
articles.summary: Britain sends Typhoon fighter jets to defend Saudi Arabia against Houthis, rules out offensive strikes  The Times of IndiaUK to deploy fighter jets to defend Saudi cities from Houthi attacks  CNBC‘Defensive role’: UK to deploy fighter planes to help ally Saudi Arabia  South China Morning PostBritain says it will carry out defensive air missions over Saudi Arabia  ReutersUK to Fly Missions to Defend Saudi Arabia From Houthi Attacks  Bloomberg.com
articles.full_text:
Britain has expanded its military support for Saudi Arabia against Yemen’s Houthi rebels, deploying RAF Typhoon jets for defensive air patrols and extending its air-to-air refuelling mission by another 90 days, Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said Tuesday.
According to the UK ministry of defence, the RAF Typhoons will conduct defensive counter-air operations over Saudi Arabia to protect cities, civilians and critical infrastructure from Houthi missile and drone attacks.
Streeting said the British aircraft would not strike Houthi targets. Britain will also send a military transport aircraft and an unspecified number of military advisers to Saudi Arabia.
According to The Associated Press, Britain had last month offered in-air refuelling support for Saudi aircraft operating against the Iran-backed Houthis.
Britain maintains a military presence across the Middle East, including RAF facilities in Cyprus and Qatar and naval facilities in Bahrain. These assets support British air and maritime operations across the region.
The Eurofighter Typhoon is a twin-engine, multirole combat aircraft developed by a European consortium involving the UK, Germany, Italy and Spain.
Designed primarily for air superiority, it can also perform ground-attack, reconnaissance and air-defence missions. 
The aircraft is operated by the Royal Air Force and several other European and Middle Eastern air forces.
Its combination of high manoeuvrability, advanced avionics and supersonic speed makes it a key component of the RAF's combat fleet.
The move comes amid a renewed escalation in Yemen’s conflict, with Iran-backed Houthi rebels stepping up missile and drone attacks against Saudi Arabia, which backs Yemen’s internationally recognised government. According to The Associated Press, the latest British deployment is aimed at strengthening Saudi Arabia’s defences against these aerial threats.

articles.title: Pakistan’s Frozen Borders: The Economic Cost Of Regional Isolation - The Friday Times
articles.summary: Pakistan’s Frozen Borders: The Economic Cost Of Regional Isolation  The Friday Times
articles.full_text:
Pakistan’s only eastern neighbor is India whereas; its western neighbors are Afghanistan and Iran. All the eastern and western borders of Pakistan are frozen because of lack of trade, commercial and travel connectivity. Only a small strip of Pakistan's northern border with China is open and that too with severe travel restrictions. With no trade with India, Afghanistan and Iran, Pakistan is a unique state because almost all its neighbors are with closed borders particularly for trade and travel purposes.
Can a state regionally isolate itself and expect to have a vibrant economy, travel and tourism? Frozen border with India is a reality since last several years and there is no direct trade and travel connectivity. Pakistan closed its border with Afghanistan and Iran which caused serious economic losses particularly in areas close to the border of the two countries. In a situation when 250 million people of Pakistan are holed up with frozen eastern and western borders, at stake is trade potential amounting to billions of dollars. There may be reasons for Pakistan to freeze its borders with India, Afghanistan and Iran, but how can a state survive in isolation particularly when its economic predicament, political instability, crisis in governance and absence of rule of law tend to add to its fragility.
Relations with India reached its lowest ebb when on August 5, 2019 New Delhi revoked the autonomous status of Jammu & Kashmir which was somewhat guaranteed under article 370 and 35-A of the Indian constitution. Since then trade, travel and all sorts of direct connectivity between India and Pakistan has ceased to exist. There is 10 billion dollars of trade potential between India and Pakistan which is advantageous to both the neighboring countries. But, unfortunately standoff between India and Pakistan continues and there is no indication for the resumption of normalization of ties and resumption of peace process. What Pakistan can do to mend fences with India by agreeing to the absorption of J&K by New Delhi and subscribing to India’s stance on terrorism? Certainly, it should be a bilateral solution and India needs to deal with the issues which it faces with Pakistan.
As far as Afghanistan is concerned, freezing of trade and closing of border has caused enormous economic losses and hardships to traders from Pakistan and Afghanistan. Whereas, Pakistan had trade surplus with Afghanistan but closing of border with its western neighbor has made things difficult for trading community of both countries. Closing of border and trade with Iran has to do with security situation in the Persian Gulf and Iran-U.S conflicts. But, trade with Iran was beneficial for Pakistan and the areas bordering Iran. Pakistan shouldn’t have come under the U.S pressure to isolate Iran and cease its trade ties with Tehran. It was because of American pressure which forced Pakistan to cease working on Iran-Pakistan gas pipeline.
 It is through trade, travel and tourism that hostility and conflicts between neighbors can be mitigated.
It means that out of four neighbors of Pakistan, three are not having normal relations with Islamabad as not only borders are closed but trade, commercial and travel ties are also affected. The cost of Pakistan’s semi or below normal ties with India, Afghanistan and Iran is an interesting phenomenon because if a country is isolated in the region it cannot have economic development or positive transformation of its economy. One can understand about Iran’s economic predicament because of its conflicts with the U.S and Arabian Gulf countries, but the economy of Afghanistan is doing well particularly in terms of value of its currency vis-à-vis U.S dollar. As far as India is concerned, freezing of trade and travel ties with Pakistan has not negatively impacted on its economy. According to the World Bank, Indian economy is rising at the rate of 7% and its foreign exchange reserves are more than 700 billion dollars. The value of Indian rupee comparing Pakistani rupee is three times. Pakistan’s economic growth rate is hardly 3.5% and its foreign exchange reserves are meager 22 billion dollars. It means that freezing of borders with India, Afghanistan and Iran is to the disadvantage of Islamabad than New Delhi, Kabul or Tehran.
One needs to analyze Pakistan frozen eastern and western borders from three standpoints. First, 250 million people of Pakistan are holed up in a country which has no connectivity with its neighbors which is having adverse social and economic ramifications. Is it not a plausible situation that out of four neighbors three are not having normal relations with Pakistan? Even China which shares a limited border with Pakistan doesn’t encourage travel connectivity with Islamabad. It means it is by default that Pakistan is facing an abnormal situation along with borders.
By engaging in diplomacy and dialogue to deal with Iran-U.S conflicts and recent armed conflict between Saudi Arabia and Yemen while freezing its trade relations with India, Afghanistan and Iran, Pakistan is not playing its cards well. Instead of Middle East, Pakistan should focus on South Asia and take steps to unfreeze its ties with India provided New Delhi reciprocates in this regard. Second, it is high time that proper research is done to estimate economic losses caused by freezing of trade with India, Afghanistan and Iran. As pointed earlier, it is not impacting on India, Afghanistan and Iran if trade with Pakistan has been suspended and borders closed. Certainly, Pakistan is losing billions of dollars every year by not having trade with three of its neighbors.
When China and India, despite having their contentious issues can have around 150 billion dollars of yearly trade and when China is India’s largest trading partner, why it has not happened between India and Pakistan? Same is true in case of Pakistan and Afghanistan and Pakistan and Iran as normal ties with their western neighbors is mutually beneficial. Particularly, if Pakistan pursues an independent approach and establishes normal trade relations with Iran by focusing on energy, Islamabad will benefit a lot. Before the suspension of Pak-Afghan trade, it was Pakistan which had trade surplus with Kabul. Therefore, it is in the interest of Pakistan to embark on survey research aiming to examine losses which Islamabad is facing by not having normal trade with India, Afghanistan and Iran. Additionally, it is not only the absence of trade with India, Afghanistan and Iran which hurts its economy, freezing of borders with three out of four of its neighbor is also negatively impacting on travel and tourism.
Finally, it is through trade, travel and tourism that hostility and conflicts between neighbors can be mitigated. Unfortunately, it has not happened in case of India and Pakistan but if there is political will and determination the two neighbors can certainly move forward in mending fences by unfreezing their borders. For that matter, it is India which needs to take an initiative and restore peace process by using dialogue and diplomacy. Political prudence exercised by the leadership of India and Pakistan by mitigating ego centric approach will go a long way in resuming trade and travel ties.
If India needs to express positive attitude with Pakistan on normalizing its relations, Islamabad need to take steps for dealing with contentious issues as far as Kabul is concerned. By closing border and restricting trade will worsen the situation. Likewise, why Pakistan has closed its border with Iran which has also ended its trade with Tehran? It is high time that strategic planning is done by Pakistan to examine how borders with its western and eastern neighbors be managed and normal trade, commercial and travel activities be resumed. Otherwise, Pakistan’s economy will be further jeopardized and brain drain of people outside the region will further intensify.

articles.title: ByteDance, Alibaba, Tencent place over $35 billion worth of Nvidia chip orders - ET Manufacturing
articles.summary: ByteDance, Alibaba, Tencent place over $35 billion worth of Nvidia chip orders  ET Manufacturing
articles.full_text:
ByteDance, Alibaba and Tencent have ordered over 3 million RTX PRO 5500 graphics cards, but Nvidia has warned it may meet only a fraction of demand as manufacturing capacity shifts towards next-generation AI data-centre systems.
US-based chipmaker Nvidia has told customers and partners it cannot guarantee that it can fill the orders because demand from Chinese technology companies far exceeds planned production, the two sources and a third person familiar with the matter said. They requested anonymity because they are not authorised to speak to the media.
The RTX PRO 5500 is a workstation chip, designed for powerful professional computers rather than the large data-centre clusters that use Nvidia's most advanced AI processors. But it is among the most powerful Nvidia chips that are still available to Chinese buyers.
One source said Nvidia told partners they might receive only 5 per cent to 10 per cent of the quantities requested. Another said the company had indicated it could produce no more than 3 million RTX PRO 5500 cards globally in 2027. Total orders from customers in China have exceeded 6 million, two of the sources said.
The three Chinese tech giants' orders are for cards priced at about $11,400 each, two of the sources said, giving them a potential combined value of more than $35 billion.
The scale of the orders, which have not been previously reported, underscores the ongoing appetite among Chinese companies for Nvidia hardware despite the US curbs.
Nvidia Chief Executive Jensen Huang has said the restrictions reduced Nvidia's share of China's AI data-centre chip market from a near monopoly to effectively nothing. But demand for the RTX PRO 5500 suggests Nvidia retains a sizeable potential market in China through less powerful products that may still be available.
The surge in demand also highlights how US restrictions have tightened computing-power supplies in the world's second-largest economy as Chinese companies race to develop cutting-edge AI models and propel Beijing's effort to deploy the technology across its industries.
Washington's curbs have pushed Chinese firms toward domestic suppliers, while Beijing has encouraged the use of homegrown chips.
Huawei, in particular, has gained market share, though Chinese chipmakers have generally struggled to match leading American products, partly because separate restrictions have limited access to the foreign equipment that is used to make the most advanced semiconductors.
An Nvidia spokesperson said Chinese producers of workstation chips and cards have experienced "unprecedented growth since 2022," when the curbs were first imposed.
"US firms continue to be restricted by a combination of outdated US export controls, which cover gaming products released nearly a half a decade ago, and China's own limit on US imports," the spokesperson said.
ByteDance, Alibaba and Tencent did not respond to requests for comment.
The US Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security, which oversees the export controls, and China's Ministry of Industry and Information Technology did not respond to requests for comment.
An export-compliant alternative
The RTX PRO 5500 is less powerful than Nvidia's H200 and B300 chips, which are designed to be linked in large numbers for the most demanding AI training and deployment workloads.
Chinese companies are seeking to use the cards primarily for AI inference, or running trained models to generate chatbot responses, the three sources said. Inference generally requires less computing power than training models on massive datasets.
The RTX PRO 5500 is similar to the RTX 6000D in performance, according to product specifications seen by Reuters.
Nvidia launched the RTX 6000D in the middle of last year as a reduced-capability product designed to meet US export restrictions. Major Chinese tech firms initially showed little interest, with some declining to place orders, Reuters reported last year.
At the time, buyers viewed the chips as overly expensive given their capabilities and hoped Washington would eventually allow sales of more powerful Nvidia processors.
Those expectations have faded as restrictions have remained in place and AI computing capacity has remained scarce, making the RTX PRO 5500 a more attractive substitute, two of the sources said.
Supply squeeze
Nvidia's inability to promise full deliveries reflects both a surge in demand and its manufacturing priorities, two of the sources said.
Starting in 2027, Nvidia is expected to devote much of its capacity at Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co to Rubin, its next-generation platform for large-scale data centres, rather than products like the RTX PRO 5500, two of the sources said. TSMC declined to comment.
Nvidia has told customers to expect early samples in December, with commercial deliveries beginning in the first quarter of 2027, they added.
The RTX 6000D has since been discontinued and its market price in China has doubled, one of the sources said.
In an October 13 filing, Shenzhen-listed fintech and AI-computing services company Tansun Technology said it had agreed to buy 20,000 RTX PRO 5500 cards from an unidentified counterparty.
It cautioned that supply shortages, industry demand and overseas technology controls could delay deliveries or reduce volumes.

articles.title: 'They chose Canada': Alberta rejects separation bid in win for Carney - The Times of India
articles.summary: 'They chose Canada': Alberta rejects separation bid in win for Carney  The Times of IndiaAlberta rejects secession referendum, chooses to remain part of Canada  CNNAlberta's decision to stay in Canada gives Carney backing to take on Trump  BBCAlberta voters reject separation from Canada in referendum  The HinduElection Day Voting Hours Extended at Multiple Locations; Results Release Delayed  Elections Alberta
articles.full_text:
Voters in Canada's oil-rich Alberta province have overwhelmingly rejected a move towards independence. They delivered a boost to Prime Minister Mark Carney's push for national unity amid US President Donald Trump's trade war and threats to annex Canada.
With more than 1.5 million votes counted, 76 per cent backed remaining in Canada, while nearly 24 per cent supported beginning the process towards separation, according to unofficial results from Elections Alberta on Tuesday. The referendum was not a direct vote on independence. Approval would have paved the way for a future vote on separation.
“Albertans made a clear choice,” Carney said, “They chose unity, to build together, and to take care of each other. Above all, Albertans chose Canada,” news agency AFP reported.
Carney said the result would allow the country to move forward together. He also called for faster efforts to diversify trade, develop major infrastructure projects and establish Canada as a global energy powerhouse, with Alberta at its centre.
Alberta Premier Danielle Smith also welcomed the early results, saying they reflected support for the province remaining within Canada.
“Albertans have voted for a stronger Alberta in a united Canada,” Smith posted on social media.
Smith had called the referendum amid growing pressure from separatists within her governing United Conservative Party (UCP), despite opposing independence. She was due to address the province on Tuesday evening about the results and Alberta's future.
The results were delayed after late openings forced more than 100 polling stations to extend voting hours on Monday.
Separatists vow to continue campaign
Despite the apparent setback, separatist leaders said the movement had gained ground and would continue to push for independence.
“We don't have the final results. I think the numbers are going to fluctuate, but it is fair to say that at least a quarter of Albertans feel that Alberta needs to be treated better,” said Keith Wilson, a leader of the separatist movement.
At a referendum night gathering in an Edmonton restaurant, supporters fell silent as the results came in. Jeff Rath of the Alberta Prosperity Project said the campaign had succeeded in bringing the issue into public debate.
“We're not going anywhere,” he said. “We've dominated the conversation in the last year. We've been educating Albertans on the benefits of independence, and we're going to continue moving forward.”
Rath had said he would be thrilled if 30 per cent of voters backed beginning the separation process. He also called for Smith to be ousted as UCP leader, warning that the party could split and potentially give rise to a new pro-independence party.
However, Thomas Lukaszuk, a former Alberta deputy premier who led the Forever Canadian campaign against separation, welcomed the outcome.
“We are a solid country that's united from coast to coast to coast,” he told supporters.
Trump's threats strengthen push for unity
Alberta is home to the world's fourth-largest proven oil reserves. The province is also a conservative stronghold whose political culture has long had more in common with the American West than much of Canada.
Resentment towards the federal government in Ottawa runs deep, but it has not traditionally translated into widespread support for independence. Separatist parties previously attracted only 1 per cent or 2 per cent of the vote, former premier Jason Kenney said.
Anger over Covid-19 restrictions helped mobilise activists who later embraced the separatist cause, Kenney said. Trump's trade war and threats to make Canada the 51st US state have since helped Carney rally support in Alberta, where Liberal prime ministers have historically been unpopular.
Carney had urged voters to deliver a decisive mandate for unity ahead of the referendum.
“Vote like Canada's future depends on it, because it does,” he told a rally in Edmonton on Friday. The city is where he grew up.
The vote also exposed the divide between separatist sentiment and concerns about the cost of living and public services.
Dustin Degenhardt, a voter in Wainwright, said Alberta had long been mistreated by the federal government.
“Alberta has essentially been treated as, you know, a colony,” he said after voting on Monday. “They want to take and take and take from us, and not return anything.”
Dave Malka, 59, of Edmonton, questioned the decision to spend money on what he called a “referendum on a referendum” instead of healthcare.
With Trump threatening Canada, Malka said, “It seems to be happening at the absolute worst time when we should be united; instead we're fighting among ourselves.”
